Figure 1.1: The ability model 
Now, let’s unpack these four branches. 
Our ability to perceive emotions is determined by how easy it is for us to identify and 
interpret our own emotions and those of others. If you are able to recognise what emotions 
are present and have an impact on a situation, regardless of whose emotions they are, then 
you would be considered as having this ability. For example, imagine that you are having a 
discussion with your team, and somebody interrupts you and starts criticising your ideas. If 
you immediately get angry and start shouting at that person, you do not have the ability to 
perceive your emotions. However, if you are able to pause and identify that you are feeling 
angry, before reacting, then you have a high competency (i.e. level of skill) to perceive your 
emotions (Mayer and Salovey, 1997: 10). In a professional context, a high competency in 
perceiving emotions means that you are able to recognise what emotions you and your 
team members are feeling, especially during times of stress or conflict.

The next branch focuses on how we can use our emotions to facilitate thought. Mayer and 
Salovey (1997: 17) describe this as ‘emotional events that assist intellectual processing’ . 
This involves us integrating our emotions into our cognitive system, and harnessing them to 
solve problems and make decisions effectively (Caruso et al., 2015: 548). This branch of 
the ability model helps us to recognise that our emotions offer valuable insights and can 
guide our cognitive functions. For example, if you are in a meeting with your manager and 
they present an unreasonable deadline for a task, you may feel an immediate stress 
response. While this emotional reaction on its own is not useful, you could use it to kick-
start a conversation with your manager about the deadline and negotiate a more feasible 
time frame. Without the initial emotional reaction, this line of thinking would not have 
occurred and you may simply have agreed to the deadline that was proposed. 
Understanding our emotions also forms part of the ability model. This means knowing 
exactly what is causing them, how they can impact a situation, and how they differ from 
and interact with other emotions (Mayer and Salovey, 1997: 13). This branch includes the 
ability to classify emotions accurately by labelling them with specific words (Caruso et al., 
2015: 548). Let’s return to the example of being interrupted in a discussion. Once you are 
able to perceive that you are angry, you can try to understand what caused it. If you 
understand that you likely felt humiliated or undermined, and that these feelings are the 
root of your anger, then you can use this information to decide how to react next.  
The final branch is managing your emotions. This is a deeper ability that can be achieved 
only once you have perceived and understood the effect of emotions on yourself and 
others correctly. This branch includes the ‘regulation of emotions to enhance emotional 
and intellectual growth’ (Mayer and Salovey, 1997: 14). Reacting to a situation purely out of 
anger would be a good example of someone who is not able to manage the overwhelming 
nature of that emotion. However, an individual who understands their emotions well would 
have a better idea of how to either soothe themself so that they no longer feel angry, or be 
able to transform it into a more conducive emotion. If we think back to our previous 
example, if you have the ability to manage and regulate your emotions effectively, you will 
realise that shouting at the other person will not improve the situation (and will likely only 
make that person angry too). Perhaps you would take a deep breath to calm yourself, and 
then ask the other person to wait until you have finished speaking before raising questions 
and concerns about your ideas.

ability not only to recognise and understand the variety of emotions we experience, but 
also to use that knowledge to navigate social situations, strengthen relationships and 
achieve goals. An individual with strong emotional intelligence is able to react to various

the ability model helps us to recognise that our emotions offer valuable insights and can 
guide our cognitive functions. For example, if you are in a meeting with your manager and 
they present an unreasonable deadline for a task, you may feel an immediate stress 
response. While this emotional reaction on its own is not useful, you could use it to kick-
start a conversation with your manager about the deadline and negotiate a more feasible 
time frame. Without the initial emotional reaction, this line of thinking would not have 
occurred and you may simply have agreed to the deadline that was proposed. 
Understanding our emotions also forms part of the ability model. This means knowing 
exactly what is causing them, how they can impact a situation, and how they differ from 
and interact with other emotions (Mayer and Salovey, 1997: 13). This branch includes the 
ability to classify emotions accurately by labelling them with specific words (Caruso et al., 
2015: 548). Let’s return to the example of being interrupted in a discussion. Once you are 
able to perceive that you are angry, you can try to understand what caused it. If you 
understand that you likely felt humiliated or undermined, and that these feelings are the 
root of your anger, then you can use this information to decide how to react next.  
The final branch is managing your emotions. This is a deeper ability that can be achieved 
only once you have perceived and understood the effect of emotions on yourself and 
others correctly. This branch includes the ‘regulation of emotions to enhance emotional 
and intellectual growth’ (Mayer and Salovey, 1997: 14). Reacting to a situation purely out of 
anger would be a good example of someone who is not able to manage the overwhelming 
nature of that emotion. However, an individual who understands their emotions well would 
have a better idea of how to either soothe themself so that they no longer feel angry, or be 
able to transform it into a more conducive emotion. If we think back to our previous 
example, if you have the ability to manage and regulate your emotions effectively, you will 
realise that shouting at the other person will not improve the situation (and will likely only 
make that person angry too). Perhaps you would take a deep breath to calm yourself, and 
then ask the other person to wait until you have finished speaking before raising questions 
and concerns about your ideas.  
Through the ability model, we can come to understand emotional intelligence as having the 
ability not only to recognise and understand the variety of emotions we experience, but 
also to use that knowledge to navigate social situations, strengthen relationships and 
achieve goals. An individual with strong emotional intelligence is able to react to various

text_resource.text:
situations in an intentional way, instead of being overwhelmed by the different emotions 
around them or within themself. This ability is crucial for any leader navigating a diverse 
workplace environment. 
The trait model 
The trait model of emotional intelligence, also known as trait emotional intelligence (trait 
EI), was developed by Petrides and Furnham (2001). This model views emotional 
intelligence as a combination of personality traits, rather than as a set of abilities or 
competencies. Furthermore, it is important to note that this model places a focus on an 
individual’s self-perception of their emotional intelligence (McCleskey, 2014: 78; and 
Petrides, 2010: 137). The trait model comprises the following four distinct components 
(Petrides, 2009: 93–95): 
1. Emotionality 
2. Self-control 
3. Sociability 
4. Well-being 
Emotionality refers to being aware of your own feelings and the feelings of others. Petrides 
(2009: 94) explains that individuals with high emotionality are able to utilise these qualities 
to establish and maintain close relationships with significant persons in their lives (e.g. 
family and close friends). In contrast, individuals with a low level of emotionality struggle to 
identify their own emotional state and communicate their feelings to others, which may 
result in less rewarding interpersonal connections. 
The next component of the trait model is self-control. This refers to having a healthy 
amount of control over your urges and desires. Individuals with a high level of self-control 
are able to control their impulses and are good at managing external pressures and stress 
(Petrides, 2009: 94). On the other hand, individuals who struggle with self-control are more 
likely to exhibit impulsive behaviour and have difficulty managing stress. 
The next component, sociability, has to do with our social relationships and social 
influence. This differs from emotionality in that it places a greater focus on the broader 
social context, rather than on our intimate personal relationships with friends and family. 
Sociability encompasses our ability to navigate social situations effectively. Individuals 
with high sociability are able to communicate and engage with people from diverse 
backgrounds. They also have good communication skills and confidence. Individuals who 
struggle with sociability appear shy and reserved in social situations and lack the ability to 
affect others’ emotions (Petrides, 2009: 94–95).

The fourth and final component of the trait model is well-being. In this context, well-being 
refers to our general feelings of happiness, positivity and fulfilment (Petrides, 2009: 95). 
Well-being extends to our achievements in the past and the expectations we have for our 
future. Individuals with a low level of well-being are more likely to feel disappointed about 
the current state of their life.

acknowledges that our emotional experiences are inherently subjective. The four 
components outlined in the trait model help us to better understand our emotions and 
serve as a guide on how we can improve our emotional intelligence. This can help us to 
enjoy stronger relationships and more effective decision-making in both our professional 
and personal lives.

3. Adaptability: This domain revolves around stress tolerance, flexibility and problem-
solving. People with a high level of adaptability can handle stress, adapt to new 
situations and find creative solutions to challenges. 
4. Stress management: This domain involves coping with emotions, tolerating stress 
and controlling impulses. Individuals who are proficient in stress management can 
handle pressure, regulate their emotional responses and make rational decisions, 
even in tense situations.

which includes happiness and optimism. People with a positive general mood are 
usually optimistic and content, and they have a positive outlook on life.

emotional and social competencies that influence an individual’s overall functioning and 
well-being. By considering domains such as intrapersonal and interpersonal skills, stress 
management and general mood, it highlights the complexity of emotional intelligence and 
its impact on various aspects of life, including personal relationships, work performance 
and overall happiness.  
Goleman-Boyatzis model of emotional intelligence 
The final mixed model that we will consider is the Goleman-Boyatzis model, which was first 
developed in 1995 (Goleman, 1996). However, it has been refined by its creators over the 
years, as they analysed more data and as research in the field developed. Goleman et al. 
(2013: 38) simplified the model to include four main domains that are closely intertwined. 
These four domains comprise various emotional intelligence competencies that contribute 
to a leader’s overall effectiveness. Goleman et al. (2013: 38) make an important distinction 
that these emotional intelligence competencies are abilities that can be learned and are 
not innate traits. They claim that each of these competencies contribute uniquely to 
making leaders more resonant and, as a result, more effective. The four primary domains 
are as follows (Goleman et al., 2013: 253–256): 
1. Self-awareness 
2. Self-management 
3. Social awareness 
4. Relationship management

text_resource.text:
we will explore the link between emotional intelligence and leadership, and how the 
different models of emotional intelligence can inform and enhance leadership practices. 
Emotional intelligence and leadership are inextricably linked and form a powerful 
partnership that defines effective leadership in the modern world (Goleman et al., 2013: 
38). Leadership is not solely about making decisions and issuing directives – it is also about 
understanding and connecting with people on an emotional, interpersonal level. To this 
end, emotional intelligence provides leaders with the essential tools to navigate the 
complex and ever-changing landscape of human interactions within organisations. 
Leaders with high emotional intelligence possess the ability to recognise and manage their 
own emotions. It is a fundamental trait that enables them to stay composed, even in 
challenging situations. This emotional self-awareness is the cornerstone of effective 
leadership (Goleman et al., 2013: 39). When leaders can manage their own emotions, they 
create an atmosphere of emotional stability, which is essential for building trust and 
inspiring confidence among team members. Furthermore, leaders with high emotional 
intelligence can empathise with the emotions of others. They listen actively, understand 
the concerns and motivations of their team members, and adjust their leadership style 
accordingly (Goleman et al., 2013: 46–47). This empathy fosters strong relationships, team 
cohesion and open communication. In addition, it helps leaders to address conflicts, 
provide support during tough times and motivate their teams to achieve common goals. 
The models of emotional intelligence show that emotional intelligence is important for 
decision-making and conflict resolution, and it provides the ability to inspire and lead with 
authenticity. As organisations face increasing complexity, uncertainty and change, leaders 
with high emotional intelligence are better equipped to guide their teams through 
challenges and achieve sustainable success. Moreover, the link between emotional 
intelligence and leadership is not a mere correlation; rather, it is a fundamental 
requirement for effective, people-centric leadership in the 21st century (Goleman et al., 
2013: 46–47). As we have seen, the prominent models of emotional intelligence that we 
have explored all contribute to leadership effectiveness in a number of ways.

Example 1 B (Emotional intelligence in the face of disruptive change) 
Sarah Mitchell, the chief executive officer (CEO) of a tech organisation, is confronted with a 
significant challenge. The organisation has been a pioneer in developing cutting-edge 
software solutions, with their flagship product being a leader in the market for a decade.

text_resource.text:
However, a competitor has recently introduced a revolutionary product that threatens to 
disrupt their market dominance. They are now facing a sudden and unexpected downturn, 
with their customers beginning to switch to the competitor’s offering. In the face of their 
competitor’s disruptive market entry, Sarah takes a methodical and poised approach. She 
refrains from hasty reactions and assesses the situation carefully, while remaining aware of 
what is at stake. 
Sarah’s unique strength lies in her emotional self-awareness. Amid the turmoil, she 
experiences a mix of fear, concern and uncertainty, both for the organisation’s future and 
for her employees’ well-being. This self-awareness forms the foundation of her emotional 
intelligence. Rather than letting her emotions dictate her actions, Sarah relies on practical 
strategies that are rooted in the mixed models of emotional intelligence. Mindfulness 
practices help her to maintain composure and manage stress. In addition, Sarah 
recognises the value of collaboration and support, and therefore, she engages her trusted 
executive team. Their collective wisdom becomes a valuable resource as they work 
together to strategise the best way forward. 
Sarah’s emotionally intelligent response yields several positive outcomes. She inspires 
confidence in her executive team and encourages open communication, so that 
employees feel confident to share their ideas and concerns. This leads to collaborative 
problem-solving. 
Under Sarah’s leadership, the organisation’s management team shifts their focus toward 
innovation. They invest in research and development to enhance their flagship product and 
explore new market segments. Sarah encourages a growth mindset, which enables the 
organisation to adapt to change and identify new opportunities. Sarah’s high emotional 
intelligence not only helps her to navigate her emotions, but also serves as a catalyst for 
positive organisational outcomes. By addressing the crisis with emotional intelligence, she 
guides the organisation toward resilience, adaptation and strategic recovery in the face of 
disruptive change. 
As you can see, emotional intelligence is the cornerstone of effective leadership, as it 
enhances a leader’s ability to perceive, understand and manage emotions – both their own 
and those of their team. By integrating emotionally intelligent principles into their 
leadership approach, leaders like Sarah can better address situations of crisis, disruptive 
change and uncertainty. This not only strengthens their leadership capabilities, but also 
fosters a resilient and emotionally intelligent organisational culture.

As you can see, emotional intelligence is the cornerstone of effective leadership, as it 
enhances a leader’s ability to perceive, understand and manage emotions – both their own 
and those of their team. By integrating emotionally intelligent principles into their

change and uncertainty. This not only strengthens their leadership capabilities, but also 
fosters a resilient and emotionally intelligent organisational culture.

In this section, we will explore various theoretical models within the realm of emotional 
intelligence and aim to illustrate the intricate ways in which emotional intelligence 
contributes to and enhances leadership efficiency, longevity and wellness. 
2.3 Theoretical foundations 
Adaptive leadership is a modern approach to leadership that was developed by Ronald 
Heifetz and his colleagues at Harvard University’s Kennedy School of Government. In this 
framework, adaptive leaders engage in various activities, such as rallying, motivating, 
organising, guiding and directing the attention of others (Heifetz, 1994: 20). Additionally, 
they assist individuals in exploring and adjusting their values. The primary goal of adaptive 
leadership is to inspire personal growth and facilitate change among individuals. 
Essentially, adaptive leadership encompasses leadership behaviours and actions that are 
aimed at assisting others in dealing with and resolving significant life changes effectively. In 
this section, we will summarise the defining characteristics of adaptive leadership. Then, 
we will evaluate the relationship between adaptive leadership, emotional intelligence and 
resilience. 
 
2.3.1 An overview of adaptive leadership 
 
According to Northouse (2016: 258), adaptive leadership is about ‘how leaders encourage 
people to adapt – to face and deal with problems, challenges, and changes’ . This approach 
focuses on managing change effectively and guiding others through it skilfully, by using the 
appropriate leadership qualities. The adaptive leadership approach is grounded in several 
key theoretical foundations, including Heifetz’s distinction between technical and adaptive 
challenges, complexity leadership theory, and behavioural psychology. The framework has 
also been developed into a leadership model by Northouse. Each of these theoretical 
foundations contributes to the effectiveness of adaptive leadership in addressing complex 
challenges and guiding organisations through turbulent times. Let’s discuss each of these 
theories in more detail.

It is important to note that challenges can also be both technical and adaptive in nature. 
These challenges are characterised by clearly defined problems, but less straightforward 
solutions (Northouse, 2016: 262). Here, an organisation may lack established rules to 
address the issue. Adaptive leadership focuses primarily on 
addressing adaptive challenges, as this is where the concept is the most useful. Leaders 
who use this approach recognise that the traditional methods and solutions used for 
technical challenges are inadequate in the face of adaptive complexities. Adaptive leaders 
acknowledge that adaptive challenges demand a more nuanced and strategic approach – 
one that encompasses a deep understanding of human behaviour, group dynamics and the 
intricacies of organisational culture. 
 
For example, consider Malik, who is the team lead of the software development 
department at his organisation. He and his team are working on a key project when, 
suddenly, a critical bug is discovered in the code. The challenge for Malik here is technical, 
because it requires specific expertise to identify and fix the bug. This is a problem that can 
be addressed through known processes, tools and expertise within the team. The solution 
involves debugging, code review and potentially rewriting a specific portion of the code. 
Now, imagine that the organisation that Malik works for is undergoing a major cultural shift 
due to a merger with another organisation. Here, the challenge is adaptive in nature, 
because it requires a shift in individuals’ behaviours and attitudes, and in the overall 
organisational culture. It is not something that Malik can fix with a simple technical

text_resource.text:
solution. Rather, he will need to navigate resistance to change, foster open communication 
and help his team to adapt to a new way of working together.  
By distinguishing between technical and adaptive challenges, adaptive leaders can guide 
their organisations through uncharted territory. These individuals lead with a deep 
appreciation for the complex nature of adaptive challenges, and they equip their teams to 
tackle these issues using innovative and human-centric approaches.  
 
Adaptive leadership and behavioural psychology 
Behavioural psychology is another foundational theory that informs the adaptive 
leadership framework. This theory revolves around understanding and analysing human 
behaviour, particularly in the context of change and adaptation. It recognises that 
individuals and groups naturally exhibit resistance to change, and that this is often due to 
fear, uncertainty or a reluctance to depart from familiar routines. Adaptive leadership 
places significant emphasis on the psychological aspects of change within organisations. 
Leaders who adopt this approach acknowledge that addressing adaptive challenges 
involves not only structural or procedural changes, but also navigating the complex terrain 
of human responses. 
In essence, adaptive leadership integrates principles from behavioural psychology in order 
to navigate the human aspect of change. As such, leaders who use this approach are 
equipped with the tools to manage emotions, address resistance and foster an 
environment that is conducive to successful adaptation. 
 
Adaptive leadership and complexity leadership theory 
Adaptive leadership also aligns with complexity leadership theory. This theory originates 
from the field of systems thinking, which posits that organisations and their challenges are 
complex and dynamic. It suggests that within any given organisation, numerous 
interconnected elements interact in unpredictable ways, resembling a complex web of 
relationships and influences. These elements include people, processes, technology, 
culture and external factors, such as market dynamics and societal trends (Obolensky, 
2014: 92–94). Complexity leadership theory encompasses administrative, adaptive and 
enabling leadership, and it emphasises strategies and behaviours that foster learning, 
creativity and adaptation within complex organisational systems. Within this framework, 
adaptive leadership is characterised as a complex process that emerges to drive adaptive 
change within a social system.

In contrast to traditional, linear and top-down approaches to leadership, complexity 
leadership theory maintains that adaptive leaders should embrace the inherent 
complexity, ambiguity and unpredictability of these challenges (Obolensky, 2014: 31). In 
other words, adaptive leaders understand that not all problems can be solved using pre-
existing expertise or established procedures. As such, these leaders often display the 
following characteristics (Obolensky: 2014: xx, 3, 40): 
• Embracing uncertainty: Rather than seek immediate solutions, adaptive leaders 
acknowledge the uncertainty that accompanies complex challenges. They resist the 
temptation to simplify issues and, instead, they consider the intricate dynamics at 
play.  
• Promoting experimentation: Adaptive leaders encourage experimentation and 
learning by empowering teams to explore various approaches. They understand that 
complex problems often require innovative solutions, and that experimentation is 
essential for discovering what works. 
• Adapting to change: Recognising that change is a constant in complex systems, 
adaptive leaders remain flexible and adaptable. They are responsive to emerging 
patterns, and they adapt their strategies accordingly. 
• Fostering collaboration: Given the interconnectivity of elements in a complex 
system, adaptive leaders prioritise collaboration and cross-functional teamwork. 
They leverage diverse perspectives in order to gain a comprehensive understanding 
of the challenges. 
• Applying systems thinking: Adaptive leaders apply systems thinking in order to grasp 
the holistic view of an organisation. By analysing how changes in one part of the 
system may ripple through other areas, they avoid unintended consequences. 
 
An important point here is that adaptive leaders must be able to manage polarities. This 
involves recognising opposing values or tensions that cannot be resolved fully in an 
organisation. Instead of seeking a one-sided solution, leaders must aim to find a dynamic 
equilibrium that balances both ends of the polarity. For example, in leadership, there is 
often tension between being directive and being inclusive. Effective leaders are able to find 
a balance between these two approaches, depending on what the situation requires. 
In essence, adaptive leadership aligns with complexity leadership theory by acknowledging 
that organisations are intricate, interconnected systems. Leaders who embrace this 
approach navigate these complexities by promoting adaptability, experimentation and

These behaviours provide general guidance for leaders as they assist others in tackling 
challenging situations and the associated changes. While there is a rough sequence for 
these leadership behaviours in the adaptive leadership process, many of the behaviours 
overlap, and leaders should demonstrate several of them simultaneously. Collectively, 
these behaviours outline a sort of blueprint for becoming an adaptive leader. 
When acted out correctly, these six behaviours should result in ‘adaptive work’ , which 
involves leaders and followers confronting change in a safe space. This safe space is 
referred to as a ‘holding environment’ , and it can be a physical or virtual space where 
individuals grapple with the adaptive challenges they face (Northouse, 2016: 273). 
Recognising the crucial role of this environment in the adaptive process, leaders should 
put substantial effort into establishing and maintaining it. 
The following are characteristics of a holding environment, which can help us to visualise 
and create it (Heifetz et al., 2009: 156): 
• A shared language to help everyone communicate effectively, as well as shared 
values and purposes 
• A history of working together 
• Vertical bonds of trusting authoritative figures and the organisational structure 
• Lateral bonds of camaraderie, trust, affection and care 
• At the micro level, a meeting room with comfortable chairs and a round table, so as 
to support the safety of confidentiality and provide an open-minded space where 
people can brainstorm and discuss respectfully 
The term ‘followers’ is often used in the context of the holding environment to refer to 
individuals who are not the leaders. However, it is important to note that this does not 
imply a submissive role in relation to the leader. This is because adaptive leadership does 
not involve leaders using their authority to control others. Instead, leaders engage with 
individuals in order to assist them in undertaking adaptive work. Therefore, in this model, 
‘followers’ is merely used to distinguish the specific individuals involved in the adaptive 
work.

It is important to remember that adaptive leadership is not a one-size-fits-all approach, but 
rather, a flexible framework that leaders can tailor to their specific challenges and contexts. 
This approach empowers leaders to navigate uncertainty, promote growth and address 
complex problems effectively, which makes it a valuable asset in today’s ever-evolving 
leadership landscape. These theoretical foundations contribute collectively to the 
development and application of adaptive leadership. Leaders who embrace this approach:  
• understand the complexity of their organisational environments;  
• can distinguish between technical and adaptive challenges;  
• address the psychological dimensions of change; 
• employ systems thinking to effect meaningful and sustainable change; and  
• act on various adaptive leadership behaviours.  
As such, adaptive leadership is a dynamic and flexible framework that is grounded in these 
foundational theories, making it well-suited for navigating the intricate challenges of 
modern leadership.

and behaviours, which cannot be accomplished through technical expertise alone.

from the immediate action in order to gain a broader perspective. This enables 
leaders to observe patterns, dynamics and underlying issues that may not be 
apparent when they are immersed in day-to-day activities. This metaphor is 
significant, because it encourages leaders to take a more strategic and reflective

easily, and the leader needs to avoid one-sided solutions. As such, the goal is to

example, in a scenario where a team needs both stability and innovation, a leader

fostering a culture of continuous improvement. Too much stability may lead to 
complacency, while an excessive focus on innovation may cause instability.

thereby ensuring a dynamic equilibrium for sustained success.

As noted in the previous subsection, adaptive leaders are skilled at distinguishing between 
technical problems with known solutions and adaptive problems that demand new 
learning, fresh perspectives and innovative approaches. However, being an adaptive leader 
is not simply about understanding change; it is also about anticipating it. An adaptive 
leader is flexible in decision-making, willing to listen and able to recognise when 
traditional, authoritative leadership styles no longer work. They possess a growth mindset, 
resilience in the face of challenges, and the ability to manage discomfort during significant 
changes. Moreover, they ‘get on the balcony’ to gain a broader perspective, manage 
polarities effectively and disturb the system when necessary, so as to foster meaningful 
change. An adaptive leader places a strong emphasis on continuous learning and 
distributes leadership throughout the organisation.  
In this way, adaptive leadership provides a practical framework that individuals and 
organisations can use to adapt to and thrive in challenging environments (Schütze, n.d.). At 
the heart of adaptive leadership is emotional intelligence. 
 
Emotional intelligence 
 
Adaptive leaders have a high emotional quotient (EQ), which means that they are able to 
understand, manage and use their emotions effectively. EQ complements adaptive 
leadership by providing leaders with the emotional awareness and interpersonal skills that 
are necessary for effective leadership. Leaders with high EQs are adept at recognising and 
managing their own emotions, as well as those of others. They exhibit empathy, which 
fosters trust and collaboration. Having a strong EQ enables leaders to navigate the 
complexities of human interactions, particularly in times of change or uncertainty 
(Goleman et al., 2013: 38). Moreover, it empowers them to inspire and motivate their 
teams, thereby fostering a positive organisational culture that is conducive to adaptability 
and growth. The following figure summarises why having a high EQ is so important for 
adaptive leaders.

Figure 2.5: How resilience empowers adaptive leaders 
 
In essence, having a high EQ and demonstrating resilience are leadership traits that 
enhance leaders’ ability to connect with their teams, navigate adversity and inspire growth. 
Leaders who embody these qualities create positive, dynamic work environments and drive 
their organisations toward long-term success. 
 
The synergy in practice 
 
In practical terms, this triad (adaptive leadership, emotional intelligence and resilience) is 
a powerful toolkit for leaders. Adaptive leadership provides the framework and strategies 
for addressing complex issues; emotional intelligence enables leaders to connect with 
others on a deeper level, and to navigate the interpersonal dynamics inherent in adaptive 
challenges; and resilience empowers leaders to stay on course and maintain their 
effectiveness, even in the face of adversity or uncertainty. 
Let’s consider an example. Imagine an organisation that is undergoing a major 
transformation – a classic adaptive challenge. Zuri, an adaptive leader, steps forward to 
diagnose the situation and mobilise the team. Her strong EQ enables her to connect with 
team members on a personal level, thereby inspiring trust and commitment. When 
challenges arise, her resilience keeps her steady, which reassures the team that obstacles 
are surmountable. This integrated approach enables Zuri to guide the organisation through 
the transformation successfully, while fostering adaptability and growth. 
The fusion of adaptive leadership, emotional intelligence, and resilience forms a dynamic 
trifecta that equips leaders with the skills and mindset necessary to thrive in our ever-
changing world. Together, they provide a road map for addressing complex challenges, 
nurturing meaningful relationships, and demonstrating unwavering resolve in the face of 
adversity. Aspiring and seasoned leaders alike would do well to embrace these three 
pillars, recognising that their synergy is the key to successful leadership in the 21st century.

2.4.1 Example 2 A 
 
A significant challenge in South Africa is the digital divide, where the economic cost and 
complexity of new technologies mean that they are not accessible to many people. Seeing 
an opportunity for social entrepreneurship, South African businessman Luvuyo Rani 
started selling used computers in Cape Town’s townships from the boot of his car. Today, 
he is a success story, and he is recognised internationally for developing a business that 
helps to create jobs and provide access to the digital economy in South Africa. As a leader, 
Rani shows how emotional intelligence and empathy can help to identify business 
opportunities that benefit stakeholders and develop solutions to challenges. 
Rani credits the resilience required to make it as an entrepreneur to his mother, who 
worked as a domestic worker and ran a shebeen from their township home in Queenstown. 
Despite traumatising police raids during apartheid, she supported her family and was able 
to send Rani and his brothers to university. Rani helped his mother during this period, 
learning about sales, suppliers and customer service (Hardach, 2018).  
Founding Silulo Ulutho Technologies 
After graduating, Rani became an accounting and business economics teacher at a high 
school in the township of Khayelitsha. In 2004, changes in the education system required 
teachers to use computers to manage administration. Many of the teachers that Rani knew 
had no computer of their own, and they lacked the computer literacy required to meet

text_resource.text:
these new demands. It was at this point that Rani noticed a business opportunity to help 
meet these needs. Resigning as a teacher, Rani and his brother started Silulo Ulutho 
Technologies by selling refurbished second-hand computers from the boot of a car. They 
travelled to different township schools across Cape Town to make sales; however, initially, 
they struggled to meet the pressure to repay debts. After engaging with customers, Rani 
decided to adopt a new approach, where Silulo provided an opportunity for groups of six 
teachers to buy computers through the use of a stokvel model, using the familiar township 
approach to financing these larger purchases collectively. This model is based on trust and 
community connections, and it was suited perfectly to meet the needs of both the 
business and its customers (Heavy Chef, n.d.; and Hardach, 2018). 
However, the technical solution of providing low-cost computers was not enough to 
overcome the challenge of digital access. Rani’s customers also needed to be able to use 
their devices. Silulo therefore expanded its offerings to courses in computer literacy and 
established a ‘one-stop shop’ for buying computers, receiving training, and repairing and 
servicing computers (Schwab Foundation, n.d.). Even with the stokvel model, there were 
people in the townships who could not afford to buy a computer of their own; however, 
these individuals needed to access the Internet. The business therefore also converted its 
premises to include an Internet café. Today, Silulo offers a wide range of courses – from 
teaching coding, to teaching soft skills – as well as employment advice and CV writing 
(Hardach, 2018; and Schwab Foundation, n.d.). 
Leading adaptively in the township context 
Many seem to view South African townships as places that are associated with 
overpopulation, poverty and crime. However, Rani argues that they are places with high 
potential and opportunities that can be accessed if people have access to connectivity and 
the Internet (Hardach, 2018).

values-driven and socially responsible approach to leadership. This is evident in the way

Sengeh reported resistance from the public to his data-driven approach to leadership

Access to education 
Sengeh later became the minister of basic and secondary education, applying his 
knowledge of designing inclusive systems to the challenges of education in the country. 
These challenges, which are complex and ambiguous, require an adaptive approach to find 
new solutions. As noted previously, the country has faced, and continues to face, many 
challenges as a result of poverty and the civil war that lasted 11 years, followed by the 
severe Ebola outbreak between 2014 and 2016. Although the government made schooling 
free in 2018, there are reports that many schools in remote areas physically punish 
students who fail to pay their school fees (Kristof, 2023).  
Making education more accessible, inclusive and effective are high-priority goals for Sierra 
Leone. Under Sengeh’s leadership, the government has begun to invest in training teachers 
and paying them more, and it now uses Sengeh’s data-driven approach to creating a series 
of controlled trials to test different schooling approaches (Kristof, 2023).  
However, a major obstacle has been a government policy, instituted during the Ebola crisis, 
that bans all visibly pregnant girls from going to public schools. The rationale behind this 
ban was claimed to be to ‘protect the students from overwhelming schoolwork and prevent 
pregnant students from being “negative influences”’ (Rodriguez, 2019). However, human 
rights and gender activists argued that this was inherently exclusionary, and was especially 
unjust to victims of sexual violence, which had increased during the Ebola outbreak 
(Equality Now, 2023). 
On the same day that Sengeh became the education minister for the country, the president 
announced that this ban would continue. Although this was a disappointment, Sengeh 
used his position in government to lobby the president to reform the policy, and he 
collected vital data to support overturning the ban (Sengeh, 2023). At the same time, other 
groups took the ban to the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) court, 
where it was found to be unfairly discriminatory. Sengeh and the government then took the 
opportunity to not only undo the ban, but also pass laws to make access to education a 
right, with a focus on access for pregnant girls and people living with disabilities (Sengeh, 
2023).

text_resource.text:
Sengeh has published a book titled ‘Radical Inclusion’ , in which he highlights the benefits 
of an empathetic approach to understanding how people are excluded, as well as the 
effect that this has on them. Although the book covers a range of topics, there are five key 
points that are raised (Sengeh, 2023): 
1. Anyone can face exclusion: Every person has experienced or will experience some 
kind of exclusion, and we can draw on this experience in order to understand how it 
affects us and others. This informs the first step of coming to understand barriers to 
inclusion fully, and what our role can be in overcoming them. 
2. You may contribute to exclusion: We may be part of the problem of exclusion – 
whether through our actions, unintended consequences or systemic approaches. 
We need to question our own assumptions and approaches, and identify how our 
beliefs, attitudes and behaviours may be contributing to certain groups feeling 
isolated and excluded. 
3. Working toward inclusion benefits everyone: Using the example of wheelchair 
ramps benefitting parents with prams, people with wheeled bags and delivery 
people, Sengeh argues that moves toward inclusion can have knock-on benefits for 
others as well. 
4. We can make a fairer world: Tackling complex challenges and divisive issues may be 
daunting; however, encountering different perspectives and debates helps to make 
us aware of new approaches that can ultimately result in a more inclusive society. 
5. The work of inclusion never ends: We need to continually innovate and refine our 
approaches in working to improve inclusivity. It is important not to take rights, 
inclusion and developments for granted. Furthermore, there can be both social and 
financial value in pursuing difficult, long-term projects to improve society.

2.5 Testing out your toolkit 
 
Consider the following fictional scenario that covers the intersection between adaptive 
leadership, emotional intelligence and resilience, and then answer the questions that 
follow. 
Durbanville General Hospital is facing a significant leadership challenge. The hospital’s 
patient outcomes have been below average consistently over the past year, which has led 
to a decline in its reputation within the community. Patients have raised concerns about 
the quality of care, with many going to private hospitals or other public institutions 
elsewhere.  
Doctor Thandiwe Khumalo, the chief medical officer (CMO), is deeply concerned about the 
hospital’s declining performance. She believes that addressing this complex challenge 
requires a comprehensive examination of the hospital’s practices, including patient care 
protocols, staff training and communication within the organisation. Thandiwe is 
convinced that the hospital’s staff members are going to need to change their approach in 
order to overcome these challenges. Her first step is therefore to get the senior staff 
members’ buy-in. She begins by calling a meeting for them to discuss the hospital’s issues, 
making sure the meeting space is comfortable, and that food and coffee are available. She 
also demonstrates vulnerability when communicating with her team, telling them that she 
wants to hear their honest feedback and ideas, with the goal of finding the best solutions.  
John Mkhize, a senior surgeon, acknowledges the challenges; however, he believes that the 
issues can be resolved quite easily, without needing much systemic change. The hospital’s 
old patient care protocols can be updated easily, so as to improve the quality of care in line 
with new standards. He also argues that hiring more nursing staff and implementing 
evidence-based nursing practices will resolve the problem quickly. Since the nursing staff 
members are stretched so thinly, they have a high level of stress, which results in a high 
employee turnover. John is sure that a larger team is all that is required to reduce this 
pressure – once this is resolved, the quality of care will naturally improve, thereby 
rebuilding community trust.  
Thandiwe then turns to the head of the hospital board, Theshaya Singh. Theshaya begins by 
agreeing with John; however, she is concerned about the impact that this expansion will 
have on the budget. Thandiwe points out that ongoing negative perceptions of the hospital 
could have an even more severe impact in the long term. Theshaya agrees with her, and 
then begins to wonder whether there are other ways they could invest the budget in order to 
improve the hospital’s performance.

Nomsa Sithole, the head nurse, adds that she feels that the issues go beyond the number 
of nursing staff. Errors and challenges arise due to poor communication between 
departments and a lack of further training across all areas of the hospital. She disagrees 
with John that the issue lies only in the number of nurses available to work. Instead, she 
feels that the surgeons contribute to the culture of high pressure that the nursing staff 
experience. The two staff members get into a heated disagreement over this. However, 
after a few minutes of debate, Thandiwe steps in to point out the similarities in their 
positions: the nurses are overworked, errors affect all departments and training is an 
essential component of addressing the problem. She eventually gets John to concede that 
many of Nomsa’s points are valid, and he agrees to collaborate with her to design new 
communications processes. 
Theshaya is pleased that their solutions are not going to stretch the budget too thinly. 
Thandiwe also gets her to agree to hire a consultant to update the patient care protocols 
and, at the same time, invest in training for all staff. This can cover both the new 
communications processes and the patient care protocols, limiting the overall expense of 
the solution. 
Exercise 2 C 
i. Critique John’s view that the challenges the hospital is facing are technical in nature. 
ii. Explain how Thandiwe uses adaptive leadership behaviours in the meeting with her 
senior staff. 
iii. Evaluate Thandiwe’s use of emotional intelligence in addressing the challenges the 
hospital is facing. 
iv. Apply the concept of managing polarities to Thandiwe’s approach toward Theshaya. 
i. While there are technical components to the challenges that the hospital faces, the 
technical challenges involve addressing the staff shortage and outdated patient 
care protocols. However, hiring more nurses poses a new problem, as the hospital’s 
budget is limited already. Furthermore, hiring more staff will not address the 
behaviour-driven challenge of poor inter-team communication. This is causing 
errors, delays and conflict between teams. Therefore, a new solution to the 
challenge will need to be found. This will most likely require the surgeons and 
nurses to change their behaviours to adapt to new communication processes. This 
challenge is therefore adaptive in nature, as it requires a more comprehensive 
solution.

ii. Thandiwe shows a number of adaptive leadership behaviours in addressing the 
challenges facing the hospital. Even before her team arrives, Thandiwe sets out to 
regulate distress by preparing the meeting space to be comfortable and welcoming. 
This helps to establish a holding environment where people feel at ease to share 
their views. She ‘gets on the balcony’ and shows that she is open to all voices. She 
does this by allowing the rest of the team space to talk, and she even invites 
different people to speak. This enables her to identify the adaptive challenges, even 
when team members are focused on only technical challenges. When tensions rise, 
Thandiwe works to maintain disciplined attention and de-escalate the conflict by 
refocusing the team members’ attention on shared views and goals. By the end of 
the meeting, her team has clear goals and has taken accountability for addressing 
the challenges. This shows that Thandiwe has given work back to the people, rather 
than try to control the changes herself. 
  
iii. Thandiwe shows a high level of emotional intelligence in her approach to this 
challenge. The hospital is facing a crisis, and tensions run high in the meeting. 
However, her approach to this is to remain composed, and to identify the underlying 
emotions and motivations of her team. She identifies points of common ground 
between Nomsa and John, helping them to see each other’s perspectives. She also 
has empathy and understands the concerns that Theshaya has around the limited 
budget, and she ensures that these are taken into account when identifying a 
solution. In this way, Thandiwe has strong social skills, and she demonstrates self-
regulation when she enables different and dissenting voices to speak in the 
meeting, so as to hear all points of view. Thandiwe’s empathy is also evident in the 
way she creates a comfortable holding environment for the meeting. 
  
iv. Managing polarities is about balancing competing needs and concerns. The hospital 
is facing serious challenges around the size of the staff and their training and 
development needs – especially with a high employee turnover in the nursing 
department. However, Theshaya has to be mindful of the hospital’s limited budget, 
given her responsibility to the board. As such, Thandiwe needs to manage the 
polarities of needing to expand and develop the nursing team, and keeping the 
hospital within its budget. She uses empathy to understand Theshaya’s position, 
and then helps to balance the two poles. She notes the long-term cost of not 
addressing the challenge sufficiently, and together, they discuss ways to address 
the challenge in a way that enables the hospital to remain within the budget.

2.6 Understanding the structure of this reader 
This unit has introduced you to the core idea for this reader – the relationship between 
adaptive leadership, emotional intelligence, resilience and wellness. Across the entire 
reader, we will explore how these concepts intersect to enable a leader to maintain 
balance and ensure longevity in an increasingly fast-paced and uncertain world. 
 
Each section of this reader contributes to this by looking at the intrapersonal and 
interpersonal skills that a leader needs in order to improve their longevity. The first section, 
‘Emotional intelligence for adaptive leaders’ , aims to introduce you to the concept of 
emotional intelligence and how it relates to adaptive leadership. We have looked at this 
concept from a theoretical and practical perspective to see how adaptive leaders deploy 
emotional intelligence in their behaviours in order to facilitate change. This section will act 
as a foundation for the rest of the reader. 
 
The second section, ‘The intrapersonal leadership toolkit’ , focuses on you as a leader, 
building on your understanding of emotional intelligence, wellness and resilience. Here, we 
will explore concepts around personal growth and strategies to develop EQ and resilience. 
Once the ideas of self-concept and self-knowledge have been explored, we will turn our 
attention to how leaders relate to other people. This makes up the third section of the 
reader: ‘The interpersonal leadership toolkit’ . Here, you will be introduced to techniques 
and skills for understanding other stakeholders – especially your followers – and how to 
relate to them. 
 
The goal of this structure is to develop a theoretical foundation to support a range of 
leadership skills and practical strategies for improving your personal resilience and 
wellness, and for understanding and engaging your followers and key stakeholders. By the 
end of the reader, you should be well equipped to lead any team through periods of 
uncertainty, empowering them as an adaptive leader and ensuring stability over time.

‘Emotional intelligence for adaptive leaders’ , aims to introduce you to the concept of 
emotional intelligence and how it relates to adaptive leadership. We have looked at this 
concept from a theoretical and practical perspective to see how adaptive leaders deploy 
emotional intelligence in their behaviours in order to facilitate change. This section will act 
as a foundation for the rest of the reader. 
 
The second section, ‘The intrapersonal leadership toolkit’ , focuses on you as a leader, 
building on your understanding of emotional intelligence, wellness and resilience. Here, we 
will explore concepts around personal growth and strategies to develop EQ and resilience. 
Once the ideas of self-concept and self-knowledge have been explored, we will turn our 
attention to how leaders relate to other people. This makes up the third section of the 
reader: ‘The interpersonal leadership toolkit’ . Here, you will be introduced to techniques 
and skills for understanding other stakeholders – especially your followers – and how to 
relate to them. 
 
The goal of this structure is to develop a theoretical foundation to support a range of 
leadership skills and practical strategies for improving your personal resilience and 
wellness, and for understanding and engaging your followers and key stakeholders. By the 
end of the reader, you should be well equipped to lead any team through periods of 
uncertainty, empowering them as an adaptive leader and ensuring stability over time.

As the previous units have established, the purpose of this reader is to explore leadership 
competencies through the lens of adaptive leadership, and to provide you with the skills 
and knowledge to thrive in leadership roles in the modern working world. In this unit, we 
will broaden our understanding of adaptive leadership and emotional intelligence by 
exploring the theoretical foundations and practical approaches to self-awareness, self-
management and self-motivation. In doing so, you will be exposed to practical tools and 
techniques that will assist you to gain a better understanding of yourself and further your 
development as an adaptive leader.

• differentiate between the concepts of self-awareness, self-management and self-
motivation; 
• analyse the relationship between self-awareness, self-management, self-
motivation and leadership; 
• discuss models and frameworks for developing self-awareness, self-management 
and self-motivation; 
• develop your own view of self-awareness, self-management and self-motivation 
through the framework of adaptive leadership; and 
• apply your knowledge of leadership, self-awareness, self-management and self-
motivation to practical cases.

lead effectively, you need to be able to ensure that your personal feelings, goals and 
challenges do not influence your decision-making and behaviour negatively. 
 
It is often the case that our personal obstacles and emotions affect our social and 
empathetic abilities. Without a proper awareness or management of ourselves, we are 
unable to interact well with others. This makes self-development the necessary first step in 
any leadership journey. Therefore, in this section, we will focus on self-awareness, self-
management and self-motivation. First, we will define and discuss these concepts in 
relation to leadership. Then, we will look at strategies to help you develop your self-
awareness, self-management and self-motivation in order to become a better and more 
adaptive leader.  
 
3.3.1 Self-awareness, self-management, self-motivation and leadership 
 
The need for change and adaptation is not new. Humans have been changing and adapting 
for millennia. However, Glover et al. [a] (2002: 16) argue that ‘the incessant rate of change 
is unique to our current time’ . The truth of this statement has increased drastically over the 
past 20 years since it was written, and the need for adaptive leadership has never been 
more vital or challenging. A leadership study based in the United States of America (USA) 
showed that for 1 939 leaders, the greatest challenges in leadership are self-awareness 
and self-motivation (Ferguson et al., 2016: 2–3). Listed as the next greatest challenge is 
managing or motivating subordinates, which is difficult if you do not have experience in 
managing and motivating yourself. These categories were chosen from a total of 17 
categories, which demonstrates the clear importance of self-awareness, management and 
motivation in leadership (Ferguson et al., 2016: 2–3). Let’s explore these three concepts in 
greater detail.

text_resource.text:
Self-awareness 
Self-awareness is the ability to understand your emotional and psychological state. The 
benefit of being self-aware is that by understanding your emotions, you can then control 
your emotional responses. At this point, it is important to note that ‘control’ does not 
necessarily mean ‘subdue’ or ‘repress’ . Our emotional responses serve an important 
biological function to help us react quickly to situations and to aid our survival (Fleming, 
2016: 7). For example, fear triggers our fight-or-flight response to keep us safe from danger.  
 
This survival mechanism also relies on the emotional responses of others to provide us 
with important information about a situation. For example, if a soldier sees someone react 
with fear, they know they are entering a dangerous situation and their body can react 
instantly. However, this instinctual emotional response presents a problem when the 
emotional reactions of others are unsuitable for the situation. This is particularly 
problematic in today’s work environment, which is characterised by emotional disruption 
due to demanding work hours, busy schedules and the continuous influx of information 
from technology. Therefore, it is important to understand where your emotional reactions 
are coming from, so that you can react to a situation appropriately. 
 
When trying to understand our emotional reactions, it is useful to turn to Eric Berne’s 
theory of transactional analysis (Fleming, 2016: 9). Transactional analysis is a 
psychological theory that aims to aid our understanding of our emotional reactions. The 
theory is based on the idea that an emotional reaction can be better understood by 
identifying the ego state of an individual during a reaction. An ego state refers to the way 
that a person is thinking, feeling and behaving at a particular time. Berne distinguishes 
between the following three ego states (Fleming, 2016: 9–10):  
1. The parent state: This ego state is influenced by the behaviours and reactions of 
parents or caretakers in a person’s formative years. 
2. The child state: This ego state is influenced by a person’s own behaviour during their 
formative years. 
3. The adult state: This ego state is assumed when behaviours and reactions occur in 
response to current experiences and stimuli.  
Let’s examine these three states further by looking at a dialogue of a hypothetical work 
scenario.

(Source: EDGE Education (Pty) Ltd, 2023; and Flaticon) 
Figure 3.2: Dialogue of a hypothetical work scenario displaying different ego states 
 
At the start of the dialogue, Ben is in the adult state. His psychological state is being 
influenced by the present moment, without subconscious interference. An emotional or a 
behavioural response in the adult state is usually rational and based on relevant 
information. In contrast, Amanda’s response stems from the child state. Her behaviour is 
being influenced subconsciously by the behaviour she learned as a child. Her reaction is 
defensive and unhelpful, and it may cause office conflict. 
At the end of the dialogue, Ben’s behaviour no longer stems from the adult state. Amanda’s 
emotional reaction, originating from the child state, has caused Ben to respond from the 
parent state. Unknowingly, his response is being shaped by the way his parents might have 
handled the situation when he was younger. Ben’s response is unhelpful, and his lecturing 
may antagonise the situation. In a work environment, for a social interaction to be 
productive and successful, both parties need to respond from their adult states, 
completely uninfluenced by behaviour that is not suitable or relevant to the situation.  
 
By understanding and recognising the ego states behind your own behaviour and that of 
others, you will be able to anticipate people’s reactions and potentially avoid 
confrontation. However, simply being aware of your emotions or ego state is not enough; 
you need to be able to control your behaviour. This is where self-management is essential.

text_resource.text:
Self-management 
Self-management is the ability to control and regulate your emotions (DuBrin, 2016: 50–
51). Self-management is often overlooked in the context of leadership, despite it being 
equally as important as self-awareness. As mentioned previously, self-awareness is an 
invaluable skill for a leader, because it enables you to understand yourself and how you 
may affect others (Miller, 2020). However, it is only with self-management that you 
can change how you affect others effectively. Again, it is important to point out that this 
does not necessarily mean subduing your emotions. This is where emotional agility comes 
into play.  
The Goleman model explains emotional intelligence as being aware of your emotions and 
not letting them affect your behaviour (DuBrin, 2016: 50–51). In contrast, emotional agility 
in leadership differs in that leaders do not try to ‘suppress their inner experiences’; rather, 
they ‘approach them in a mindful, values-driven, and productive way’ (David and 
Congleton, 2013). In other words, an emotionally intelligent leader focuses on preventing 
their emotions from affecting their behaviour, whereas an emotionally agile leader allows 
their emotions to affect their behaviour in a correct and productive manner. One could say 
that self-awareness is a practice in emotional intelligence, and that self-management 
requires a combination of emotional intelligence and emotional agility. Self-management 
is crucial for adaptive leadership, because it enables us to ‘achieve our goals, achieve self-
growth and professional growth, and take care of our emotional well-being’ (Davis, 2022). 
However, effective self-management requires the dedication and perseverance that come 
from self-motivation.  
 
Self-motivation 
Self-motivation refers to an internal drive to strive for and achieve set goals and objectives 
(Emamzadeh, 2022). It is important for a leader to understand self-motivation and where it 
stems from. Discussions about self-motivation often distinguish between intrinsic 
motivation and extrinsic motivation (Ackerman, 2018). Can you recall an instance where 
you have procrastinated on a task set by a teacher or an employer? Compare this to the 
times you have done a task that you set for yourself – perhaps an activity for one of your 
hobbies. Did you find the second task easier to complete than the task in the first 
situation? Here, the first situation is an example of extrinsic motivation. This is when you 
are motivated to do something by external motivators, such as following instructions from 
a teacher. The second situation is an example of intrinsic motivation, which is when you 
complete a task that you have chosen to do because you enjoy it.

text_resource.text:
Leaders are often more likely to be driven by extrinsic motivation due to their demanding 
position. For example, a leader may have a greater workload or a greater need for social 
status that compels them to work harder. This is not ideal for an effective leader, because 
extrinsic motivation may not be meaningful or fulfilling, making it unsustainable in the long 
run. Because self-motivation is typically driven by intrinsic motivators, it is usually more 
meaningful and sustainable. However, while self-motivation stems mostly from intrinsic 
motivation, it can also stem from extrinsic motivation. In fact, most people experience a 
combination of intrinsic and extrinsic motivation for different aspects of their lives 
(Ackerman, 2018). As such, an adaptive leader needs to understand what self-motivation 
is, so that they can identify it and try to replicate it in the facets of their life where they may 
lack sustainable motivation. 
Understanding these concepts will enhance your personal growth and transform you into a 
more effective and adaptive leader. The next step is to gain first-hand experience by 
practising the strategies and techniques associated with these concepts. This will further 
your self-development and give you the ability to personalise your advice and leadership to 
others. In the following subsections, we will explore a few of these strategies and 
techniques.

There are many different strategies for developing self-awareness, many of which are also 
helpful for maintaining self-management and self-motivation. Due to the personalised 
nature of this topic, there are no clear correct or incorrect techniques that are 
conventionally agreed upon, and it is up to you to experiment and see what works best for 
you. For the purposes of this unit, several of the most popular techniques have been 
divided into three categories, as shown in the following figure.

text_resource.text:
Figure 3.3: Strategies for developing self-awareness 
 
Reflection 
The logical initial step in developing self-awareness as a leader is to reflect on your own 
behaviour, character, thoughts and emotions. This can be done through introspection and 
double-loop learning. 
Introspection 
The first form of self-evaluation is introspection. This is essential for developing self-
awareness; however, it is not accomplished easily (Miller, 2020). In the context of adaptive 
leadership, Glover et al. [a] (2002: 28) advocate for a critical approach that involves 
questioning the foundational assumptions on which organisations make their decisions. 
This perspective suggests that effective leadership entails questioning what is ‘true’ . By 
doing so, organisations are able to act adaptively by putting aside outdated assumptions, 
biases or prejudices, if the situation requires it. 
 
This same practice should be applied to introspection in self-awareness development. 
Questioning your self-knowledge can provide you with new information, thereby making 
self-awareness more attainable. A useful technique to assist you is to keep a thought diary. 
Here, you should record only factual details, without providing emotional context that may 
cloud your interpretation (Miller, 2020). For example, if you were involved in an argument at 
the office, try to write down the exact words you said, without adding why you said them. 
Introspection also ties in well with double-loop learning.

text_resource.text:
Double-loop learning  
Double-loop learning is a concept designed to teach people ‘to think more deeply about 
their own assumptions and beliefs’ (Cartwright, 2002: 68). DuBrin (2016: 485–486) 
describes the difference between single-loop and double-loop learning as differences in 
‘levels of self-awareness’ . Single-loop learners ‘seek minimum feedback’ , while double-
loop learners engage in in-depth analysis by confronting the validity, values or efficacy of 
things (DuBrin, 2016: 485–486). In other words, just like introspection, double-loop learning 
is about analysing and questioning what is believed to be known.  
This is useful for an adaptive leader, since it reinforces the benefits of introspection while 
you engage productively with failure through analysis and feedback (DuBrin, 2016: 486). 
For example, if you are a team leader and you fail to lead your team effectively, you may 
question your self-perception and your leadership abilities, and you may ask for feedback 
from the team. By doing so, you are less likely to make the same mistake. Acquiring 
feedback through double-loop learning ties in with other methods of seeking feedback.  
 
Feedback 
Feedback is a crucial part of developing self-awareness, since we are incapable of 
considering ourselves without bias. There will always be blind spots in our self-perception, 
which makes it necessary to seek assistance on our self-development journey. Two 
techniques that can assist with this are the Johari Window model and a mentor/support 
system. 
 
One way to counter our blind spots is by using the Johari Window model (Fleming, 2016: 
32–34). In this model, different pieces of information about you are represented within four 
blocks called ‘areas’ , two of which contain information known to you, while the other two 
are unknown. This model is summarised in the following figure.

As you can see, the Johari Window model is one that requires assistance for it to be most 
effective, as the purpose of the model is to uncover information about you that is unknown 
to you but known to others. However, it can sometimes be an emotionally distressing 
experience when the feedback is critical. It is therefore important that you have a mentor or 
a strong support group whose advice you can trust and respect. 
 
Mentor/support system  
As mentioned previously, a good way of developing self-awareness is through feedback 
from others to compensate for our cognitive prejudices and blind spots (DuBrin, 2016: 
486). It is important to accept feedback whenever you receive it and, most importantly, to 
learn to accept criticism. Of course, dealing with criticism is an emotionally volatile aspect 
in the workplace – giving and receiving criticism are difficult, and both require proper self-
awareness. This is made easier by finding a mentor, who should preferably be someone of 
a senior age or position in the same organisation or field of work. Alternatively, or 
additionally, you should try to build a support system of friends, family and co-workers who 
can give you advice and feedback in a more informal and comfortable way. The information 
you learn from others can also help you to better identify your values and abilities.

To be a successful and productive leader, it is important for you to achieve self-
identification by knowing your values and your abilities (i.e. your strengths and limitations) 
(Young, 2022: 54). 
Values 
When trying to develop your emotional agility, an important step is to assess your values 
(Fleming, 2016: 4). Understanding your values may help you to identify the cause behind 
certain behaviours and emotional reactions (Fleming, 2016: 6). For example, you may have 
lashed out at someone because what they said offended one of your core values. 
Furthermore, identifying and understanding your values can help you to make the right 
decisions for your work and personal life (Young, 2022: 56). For example, if you believe in 
integrity and honesty, then working in a corrupt environment will bring you only distress, 
and it is less likely that you will be able to lead successfully. 
 
Abilities 
Identifying your strengths and weaknesses is a beneficial quality in a leader (Young, 2022: 
54). It allows for a level of self-awareness that will help you to be realistic about your 
behaviour, abilities and potential. For example, if you have strong communication skills, 
then you will do well in a job that requires a lot of social interaction, such as working in 
sales. Alternatively, if you struggle with public speaking, then you would be better suited to 
a job that does not require giving large presentations. While knowing your limitations can 
help you to make the correct career decisions, it can also show you on which areas you 
need to focus to improve your self-development. However, you should not do so at the 
expense of your strengths. Rather than obsess over a personal limitation, you should 
choose tasks that play to your strengths and seek help when working within the areas of 
your limitations. For example, if you are not a naturally organised person, then try to 
compensate by using an organisational app.  
 
While there are many other techniques to develop your self-awareness, this is a good place 
to begin. Moreover, improving your self-awareness will teach you how to be more aware of 
others, which is required for effective adaptive leadership in a work environment that is 
characterised by unexpected obstacles and emotions. Once you have begun your self-
development journey by putting self-awareness tools and techniques into practice, it is 
important to maintain these practices. This can be done through self-management.

3.3.3 Strategies for practising self-management 
 
It is important to understand that self-management is a holistic practice. This means that it 
includes regulating and maintaining your psychological and physical health, as well as your 
actions, emotions and behaviour. In this subsection, we will consider a few of the 
strategies you can use to manage your emotions, actions and behaviour, and your physical 
and emotional health. 
 
Managing emotions 
To initiate the process of regulating your emotions, you need to start by monitoring and 
managing your emotions. Of course, the first step in monitoring your emotions is to identify 
what you are thinking and feeling through self-awareness techniques. This means that self-
management is nearly impossible without self-awareness. The two concepts need to work 
hand in hand. A useful model to understand how these two concepts can work together is 
Plutchik’s wheel of emotions, which can be seen in the following figure (Fleming, 2016: 21–
23).

text_resource.text:
Figure 3.5: Plutchik’s wheel of emotions 
 
As you can see in the figure, the wheel of emotions includes a variety of emotions that are 
separated by different sections and rings. The purpose of this model is to help you predict 
the direction in which your emotions may progress if they are left unchecked. Plutchik 
based this model on the distinction of eight primary and eight advanced emotions 
(Fleming, 2016: 21–22). The primary emotions are set in the middle ring, while the 
advanced emotions are set in the inner ring. The darker shade represents the intensity of an 
emotion, and the emotions outside of the circle (marked by arrows) are the result of 
combining two emotions from adjacent segments.

text_resource.text:
Let’s consider an example. Kate feels bored with her job. If this boredom is left unchecked, 
it may develop in intensity and turn into disgust with her work. Again, if left unchecked, 
Kate’s emotions will fester and she will eventually loathe going to work. Furthermore, 
imagine that Kate chose this job that she hates over a better opportunity and is now sad 
about her decision. The consequent emotion she will experience is remorse. By using self-
awareness techniques and Plutchik’s wheel of emotions, Kate will be able to identify her 
emotions and their underlying causes, and predict what may happen if the situation 
continues. Even if Kate is not able to change her situation, at least she will be prepared for 
the predicted emotional development, and she will be in a better position to manage her 
emotions and behaviour. 
Now that you understand how to monitor your emotions, you can practise managing your 
emotions and emotional responses. One of the most effective ways to do this is to prepare 
in advance when you know you will be put in a stressful situation. For example, if you have 
an important meeting coming up, be aware that stress may cause you to have a strong 
emotional reaction. Once you are aware of a possible emotional response, you can think of 
ways to manage your response in the moment. Consider the following tips to keep in mind 
in the heat of the moment, to help you regulate your emotions and emotional responses 
(Fleming, 2016: 53–54): 
• Before speaking or reacting, consider your ego state and act accordingly. 
• Take ten seconds to calm down with deep breathing. 
• Accept and acknowledge what you are feeling, even if it is anger. 
• Try to consider how your reaction or behaviour will affect others.  
By preparing yourself mentally and considering ways to avoid losing control in advance, you 
are more likely to remain composed and productive during a tense or provocative work 
situation. Remaining composed in order to be an effective and professional leader can be 
further assisted with techniques to help manage your behaviour.  
 
Managing behaviour 
Remaining calm and ensuring the continuation of productive behaviour in the face of chaos 
is a necessary leadership trait. It is therefore important that you learn how to manage your 
behaviour so that it aligns with your responsibilities and goals. This means that in addition 
to managing your behaviour through regulating your emotions, you also need to manage 
the way you conduct yourself during periods of turmoil. Let’s look at a few techniques to 
help you achieve this.
