Time management and organisation  
In the development of effective self-management, time management and organisation are 
as important as emotional regulation. When you are experiencing a difficult time in your 
work or personal life, it is easy to feel lost and overwhelmed. Through time management 
and organisation, you can manage some of the chaos, while giving yourself a sense of 
control over your life. This will improve your ability to be efficient and productive (Davis, 
2022).  
To help yourself become more organised, try creating lists of everything going on in your 
life. It can be overwhelming to see everything you need to resolve or accomplish at once, so 
try to separate different aspects of your life into their own categories. For example, you 
could separate your personal obstacles or errands from your work obstacles or tasks. By 
doing so, it will be easier to prioritise and work out a suitable schedule. To make your 
organising and time management more adaptive, try creating a weekly plan based on your 
to-do list, and include all the important dates and deadlines from your calendar (Davis, 
2022). Make sure that you update the weekly plan regularly, so that you can adjust to any 
unexpected obstacles or delays. 
 
Focus and visualisation 
Self-management requires intent and willpower to achieve. If you are struggling to find the 
energy or drive to focus on and follow through with self-awareness and self-management 
practices, then you will need to find inspiration from somewhere to help guide you. A useful 
technique is through vision and conceptualisation. For example, if you are in a leadership 
position and you are struggling to manage yourself effectively, then envision your ideal 
leader. Consider what strengths, values and weaknesses they might have and how they 
might respond in your situation. Then, try to regulate your behavioural and emotional 
responses so that they mimic those of your envisioned ideal leader (DuBrin, 2016: 487). 
This is another example of why having a mentor can be beneficial to your self-
development.

request progress reports from your mentor, manager or co-workers. As a leader, it is 
important that you demonstrate a desire for progression and accomplishment. By 
reviewing feedback from others, you will gain a better understanding of your self-
management progress and how your behaviour is perceived by others. 
However, keep in mind that self-management is a holistic practice. In other words, self-
management includes managing every aspect of your life. Managing your emotions and 
behaviour will get you only so far if you neglect your health, which will inevitably create 
more stress and disruption. To this end, we will now discuss a few concepts to help you 
manage your health. 
 
Managing physical and psychological health 
 
We have already seen how adaptive leadership requires emotional intelligence, and how 
emotional intelligence requires self-management. However, effective self-management 
cannot be achieved without maintaining your well-being. If your psychological or physical 
health is compromised, then you will not have the strength or resilience to encounter 
obstacles with composure and clarity of thought. Now, let’s explore a few strategies that 
can help you to maintain your status as a healthy and strong leader. 
 
Practise ‘kaizen’ 
Leaders often neglect their physical and psychological health due to the greater work 
demands of their position. It is unsustainable to continue to push yourself when you 
neglect your health. This is because, at some point, your body or your spirit will weaken, 
and you may fall ill or have an emotional crisis. Therefore, it is essential to practise self-
care, which is a concept crucial for coping with continued self-management. The first step 
in self-care is not to take too much on at once. When discussing the fundamental skills for 
adaptive leadership, Glover et al. [b] (2002: 30) refer to a Japanese concept called ‘kaizen’ , 
which is a business philosophy where organisations and employees work together to 
accomplish ‘slow continuous improvements’ . The same approach should be taken in your 
self-development journey. It is not enough to practise self-awareness once and then leave 
it at that. However, you should also not do too much at once. Instead, you should practise 
‘kaizen’ and continue to practise self-awareness techniques to improve your self-
management slowly but steadily.

Practise mindfulness 
Mindfulness is a growing psychological, cultural and spiritual phenomenon that has many 
different uses in self-development and adaptive leadership. Practising mindfulness assists 
your cognitive ability to stay in the present moment and focus on the task or problem at 
hand (Ruderman et al., 2022: 33). Even on an ordinary day, leaders juggle various 
responsibilities and distractions, thereby risking errors, because they are stressed or 
overwhelmed. By practising mindfulness, leaders can give themselves an advantage in 
dealing with expected or unexpected chaos. There are many ways to practise mindfulness, 
and many of them can be done in any place or for any period of time. Starting small is 
recommended – i.e. briefly pause every couple of hours and focus on the present moment 
for a few minutes. Another effective method is to sit outdoors and focus on your senses 
one at a time – i.e. consider what you are feeling, hearing, smelling, seeing or tasting in a 
particular moment (Ruderman et al., 2022: 82). 
 
Exercise 
The benefits of exercise on physical and psychological health are numerous. Due to their 
increased burdens, leaders often struggle with chronic stress, which affects their cognitive 
abilities and immune system. For example, excessive stress causes an imbalance in the 
body’s hormonal system that results in stress-related hormones, such as adrenaline, being 
released too often (Ruderman et al., 2022: 28). Physical exercise is an effective method to 
eliminate any excess hormones, giving you a greater opportunity for emotional and physical 
stability and well-being. Physical exercise is also an effective way of taking a timeout when 
you are feeling emotionally compromised. For example, during a stressful day at work, you 
could take a brisk five-minute walk in between meetings to help distract you from your 
problems and counter any stress-related hormonal imbalances.  
All the strategies listed in this subsection can be accomplished with minimal effort and 
time constraints. However, for them to have any effect on your self-development as a 
leader, you need to ensure that you practise them regularly. This is where self-motivation 
becomes essential.

text_resource.text:
self-development and adaptive leadership, since it can affect your ability to engage in and 
follow through with self-awareness and self-management practices (Ackerman, 2018).  
Earlier in this unit, we looked at Goleman’s framework for emotional intelligence, which 
includes motivation. Goleman explains motivation by focusing his theory on the following 
four fundamental aspects (Ackerman, 2018):  
1. Achievement drive 
2. Commitment 
3. Initiative 
4. Optimism 
Let’s explore each of these aspects in more detail. 
Achievement drive 
Your achievement drive refers to your compulsion or desire to ‘achieve, improve, and meet 
certain standards’ (Ackerman, 2018). For example, the reasons for why you want to change 
something would fall under the umbrella of achievement drive. When you are struggling to 
feel motivated, you should try to focus on your achievement drive in order to see if there is 
anything you can do to ignite a metaphorical fire within yourself. For instance, you could 
visualise yourself achieving your objective to try to inspire some passion within yourself. 
Commitment 
Commitment to your goal is something that does not always come naturally or easily. 
Desire plays a great part in commitment by initiating your journey to reach a certain goal.

2. Commitment 
3. Initiative

Your achievement drive refers to your compulsion or desire to ‘achieve, improve, and meet 
certain standards’ (Ackerman, 2018). For example, the reasons for why you want to change 
something would fall under the umbrella of achievement drive. When you are struggling to 
feel motivated, you should try to focus on your achievement drive in order to see if there is 
anything you can do to ignite a metaphorical fire within yourself. For instance, you could 
visualise yourself achieving your objective to try to inspire some passion within yourself. 
Commitment

reach your goal. Glover et al. [b] (2002: 22–24) list the following four predisposing

such a case, you may not be able to achieve your goal, despite your commitment. This can

health, which may, in turn, compromise your ability to self-manage.

Figure 3.6: Setting SMART goals 
 
As you can see, setting SMART goals is about being specific and organised. Following this 
framework can help you to set and achieve attainable goals. Achieving these goals will fuel 
your self-motivation and assist you in whatever you set out to do, including leadership 
development. When we do not set realistic goals, then the disappointment of failure can 
have a catalyst effect, which may affect our self-motivation and our ability to self-manage. 
As such, self-awareness is also an essential quality to have when setting your SMART 
goals.

self-motivation. By incorporating these techniques into your daily life, you can improve your 
emotional intelligence and, in turn, increase your potential to be an effective adaptive 
leader. In the following sections, we will explore examples of how these techniques may 
assist you in your future leadership roles.

3.4.2 Example 3 B 
 
Educators perform an important role in providing students with the knowledge, skills, 
strategies and attitudes necessary to succeed in the workplace. It is therefore important for 
educators to have a good understanding of emotional intelligence to ensure successful 
leadership, both for themselves and for their students. To understand the importance of 
emotional intelligence in educational leadership, a study conducted in the Ugu district of 
KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, explored the emotional intelligence strategies of five female 
school principals (Mlangeni, 2014: vii). Basing its research on the Goleman emotional 
intelligence model, the study looked specifically at the participants’ engagement with self-
awareness, self-management, social skills and self-motivation (Mlangeni, 2014: 26).  
From the study, it became clear that all the participants believed that understanding one’s 
strengths and weaknesses facilitates their ability to manage their emotions. Furthermore, 
Mrs Nguse, one of the school principals, stated that self-awareness is important to her in 
terms of knowing what makes her happy or angry. This is based on the idea that such 
knowledge can prevent her from being caught off guard by an unexpected emotional 
reaction. Mrs Nguse also stated her belief that having a positive attitude toward receiving 
feedback is essential for leading teachers and students. Her argument was that by 
considering criticism as constructive and helpful, you are more likely to learn and less 
likely to make the same mistakes (Mlangeni, 2014: 56). 
All of the principals agreed to the importance of being able to regulate their emotions, 
which they achieved through the following practices (Mlangeni, 2014: 52–55): 
• Taking time out 
• Redirecting their energy 
• Acknowledging their emotional strengths and weaknesses

Strategies for taking time out included walking away from the person or situation that has 
distressed them. Alternatively, a few of the principals decided to ‘walk around, take a deep 
breath or drink water in order to calm down and deal with the matter later’ (Mlangeni, 2014: 
52). 
All five of the principals stressed the importance of self-motivation in their position as 
leaders, citing (Mlangeni, 2014: 50–51): 
• its effects (such as increased positive emotions) that they, as leaders, then transfer 
to their colleagues; 
• the ability to motivate their colleagues; 
• the ability to work under pressure; and  
• the ability to create a productive work environment.

4.1 Introduction 
 
In Unit 3, you learned about self-awareness, self-management and self-motivation theories 
and techniques. Having a clear understanding of these concepts will help you to grasp the 
Comprehensive Resilience (CORE) framework, which we will discuss in this unit. This 
framework is especially important in relation to understanding the concept of resilience 
and its importance in leadership. By explaining the value of and need for resilience 
practices and techniques, this unit will provide you with the theoretical knowledge and 
practical skills necessary for you to build resilience and become a more effective and 
adaptive leader. The discussion in this unit links in well with Unit 5, where you will learn 
how these practices can also assist in terms of your well-being and your ability to manage 
stress.  
After studying this unit, you should be able to: 
• define resilience; 
• analyse the relationship between resilience and leadership; 
• discuss the CORE framework as a means to develop resilience;  
• develop your own view of resilience through the framework of adaptive leadership; 
and 
• apply your knowledge of leadership and resilience to practical cases.  
 
4.2 Key terms and definitions 
 
The following key terms and definitions apply to this unit: 
• Bias: A preconceived and unsubstantiated opinion, thought or attitude toward 
someone or something. While often used in a negative context, a bias can be 
positive, negative or neutral. 
• Cognitive bias: The brain’s systematic error in thinking when thought patterns are 
filtered through the personal experiences and preferences that someone has 
accumulated over the course of their lifetime.  
• Cognitive performance: The speed, effectivity and abilities of the brain in the context 
of processing, acquiring, manipulating or producing information.

should be addressed. Let’s explore the concept of resilience further by examining a few of 
these misconceptions and considering how they can be re-evaluated. 
 
Bouncing back 
The first misconception is the commonly held belief that resilience is simply about being 
able to ‘bounce back’ from adversity. In their discussion on resilience, Ruderman et al. 
(2022) criticise this interpretation. Rather, they believe that resilience is more than merely 
avoiding or recovering from adversity – it is about being able to grow during times of 
challenge. Furthermore, there is an argument that the idea of ‘bouncing back’ can alienate 
some people. This is because it implies quick and effortless recovery when, in fact, it takes 
many people months or years to recover from adversity, while some find it almost 
impossible to do so in extreme circumstances (Neenan, 2018: 5). In these circumstances, 
it is important to understand the diverse and adaptable nature of resilience, as well as how 
it can be applied to different aspects of your life.  
Trial by fire 
Trial by fire involves the idea that the descriptor ‘resilient’ can be applied to you only after 
you have endured adversity. In other words, it implies that people consider developing 
resilience only after a challenge has occurred, or that someone is considered resilient only 
if they have endured something and bounced back from it (Coutu, 2017: 6). This is linked 
closely to another misguided belief that people are either resilient or they are not. However, 
resilience can be learned. In other words, it is not dependent on genetics, social upbringing 
or experience, although those aspects do help (Coutu, 2017: 10). Furthermore, resilience 
does not have to be an afterthought or an innate (natural) characteristic. By understanding 
resilience and practising thought-out and individualised techniques to develop resilience in 
different areas of your life, you can consider yourself resilient before going through 
adversity and proving it.  
 
Staying positive  
Another common misconception is that resilience means having an optimistic nature. With 
this view, it is believed that someone who consistently views the glass as half full rather 
than half empty is more likely to be resilient. Often, people are told that if they have a 
positive mental attitude and emotional outlook on life, they can overcome anything. 
However, although having an optimistic outlook in life is certainly beneficial, it can also be 
dangerous if it is not also tempered by a realistic perspective (Coutu, 2017: 11). For this

positive mental attitude and emotional outlook on life, they can overcome anything. 
However, although having an optimistic outlook in life is certainly beneficial, it can also be 
dangerous if it is not also tempered by a realistic perspective (Coutu, 2017: 11). For this

reason, it is crucial to practise different resilience strategies. By relying on only one 
strategy, you may be unable to endure an obstacle that requires a different perspective or 
approach. For example, if you rely on only having a positive outlook, then you may not be 
equipped to deal with a negative situation, such as having to inform a staff member that 
they are being retrenched. In order to achieve effective resilience, you need to take a 
holistic approach and work on becoming more resilient in every area of your life.  
As we can see through our exploration of different definitions of resilience and re-
evaluating outdated ideas, it is evident that resilience is a complex and multifaceted 
concept – i.e. there are many different aspects or sides to it. In the following subsection, we 
will discuss how the concept of resilience can assist you in becoming an adaptive leader.

within the context of occupational challenges and leadership. Research shows a 
correlation between resilience and effective leadership, as well as perceived work

shows in individuals’ performance and behaviour as perceived by others. Unfortunately,

Originally used by the American military to describe the destabilised global conditions 
following the end of the Cold War, this concept has since been repurposed and featured in 
discussions on leadership theory and development (Young, 2022: 2). In VUCA situations, 
leaders need to be resilient in terms of obstacles that are thrown at them. This requires 
leaders to know how to use their resources wisely, which can be done by using a resilience 
portfolio. 
A resilience portfolio is a strategy that is used for developing resilience, and it is managed 
similarly to how a financial portfolio is managed. It involves allocating resources in the 
present moment in order to build a more resilient future. For example, when you engage in 
resilience practices, you are essentially investing your current resources (like time and 
effort) to strengthen yourself for future challenges. Similar to diversifying assets in an 
investment portfolio for maximum growth potential, it is crucial to vary the resilience-
building strategies that you make use of in your resilience portfolio. This approach ensures 
that you develop well-rounded resilience that can help in a variety of situations (Ruderman 
et al., 2022).  
The importance of cultivating and preserving resources within effective leadership cannot 
be overstated. The danger of excessive demands experienced by leaders can often lead 
to loss cycles, where resources are lost or mismanaged, thereby impairing your ability to 
function as an effective leader and as an individual. However, by practising resilience and 
investing in your resilience portfolio, you can create gain cycles, where resources are 
gained. Importantly, both loss and gain cycles are self-generating. This means that if you 
experience a loss cycle, it will continue, unless you take action. Fortunately, because gain 
cycles are also self-generative, by practising resilience, you will generate more resources, 
strengths and abilities. This, in turn, will generate even more resources. For example, by 
practising healthy sleep patterns, you will generate the resource of energy levels, and high 
energy levels will enable you to accomplish more or generate more resources.

text_resource.text:
i. Resilience is a multifaceted concept that incorporates the idea of being able to 
withstand or recover from adversity, while becoming stronger in the process. This 
may include improving your abilities, potential and psychological strength. 
  
ii. In order to be an effective adaptive leader, you need resilience. You need to be able 
to adjust to changes quickly and persevere when faced with obstacles. Resilience 
equips you with the necessary strength and wisdom to navigate obstacles, without 
sacrificing the vital resources that are required to lead effectively. One cannot be a 
leader without resilience, as it contributes to work performance, how employees 
perceive you, and how well you can work under pressure. It demonstrates a positive 
attitude, willingness and the drive for success in the workplace. If you are leading by 
example, these are the attributes you need in order to be successful at it. 
  
iii. VUCA stands for volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous. It is an acronym that 
has been repurposed from its original military use, and it is now used in the context 
of business and leadership challenges to refer to the unpredictability and 
turbulence common in the modern work environment. Due to the diversity of 
problems and obstacles that arise in these VUCA environments, leaders need to be 
resilient, so that they can handle the stress and adapt to new and challenging 
situations quickly.  
  
iv. Answers may vary. The following serves as a guide. 
 
A resilience portfolio is a way of understanding how to cultivate resilience. 
Performing resilience practices can be likened to investing in a financial portfolio. It 
involves taking the time now to spend certain resources in order to benefit you in 
your future. For example, during a stressful period in your life, taking the time to do 
exercise requires using up one of your current precious resources – i.e. your time – 
and putting it toward future benefits by strengthening your body. An important 
aspect of the resilience portfolio, like an investment portfolio, is to diversify your 
assets as much as possible, so as to ensure maximum growth potential. For 
example, exercising and meditating helps both your body and your mind, thereby 
creating a more well-rounded resilience. In this way, if you sustain an injury and 
cannot exercise, then at least you can still meditate, which will ensure that you still 
have a means of managing your stress.

Sleep 
Sleep, like exercise, affects your attentiveness and alertness – both of which are vital 
qualities in an effective leader. Studies have shown that sleep deprivation can affect an

text_resource.text:
individual’s cognitive performance ‘to the same degree as 0.1 percent blood alcohol 
concentration’ (Ruderman et al., 2022). This can have serious consequences, including 
falling asleep while driving or making mistakes at work, which can affect the lives of many 
to different extents. For example, the Chernobyl nuclear accident is thought to have been a 
result of human error, due largely to the sleep deprivation of the power plant workers 
(Ruderman et al., 2022). While Chernobyl is an atypical example, it is likely that as a leader, 
your sleep deprivation can affect others, as your behaviour and decisions have an impact 
on your staff or subordinates.  
Research indicates that many leaders do not get enough sleep, with work demands, 
constant digital communication and an imbalance between work and personal life 
contributing to the problem. This can have a significant impact on their resilience – 
particularly the social aspect of the CORE framework. This is because sleep deprivation 
directly influences how leaders perceive and react to others’ emotions. For example, when 
an individual is deprived of sleep, they tend to respond to difficult situations more 
negatively. Furthermore, sleep deprivation is associated with heightened workplace stress 
(Fernandez et al., 2020: 7). 
The following can be done to help you have a lengthier and sounder sleep (Fernandez et al., 
2020: 7): 
• Keep a consistent sleep schedule: This is the fastest way to healthier sleep and 
increased energy levels, as your sleep patterns can affect your biological alarm 
clock. It is possible for you to set your body’s alarm clock to the times you want by 
following a consistent sleep schedule. 
• Create a sleep routine: You should try to ensure that you do not engage in any 
activities directly before bed that may stimulate your brain or your body. For 
example, you should not exercise, drink stimulating beverages or expose yourself to 
blue light (such as a mobile phone or laptop screen) directly before going to bed. 
• Try to control your sleep environment: Most people need a quiet and dark sleeping 
environment. Therefore, if you need to, try eye masks or blockout curtains to ensure 
maximum comfort and minimal disturbances. You should also ensure that you are 
physically comfortable by prioritising the purchase of a good-quality mattress and 
pillows, if possible. 
There are numerous benefits of ensuring healthy sleep habits. Unfortunately, for many 
people, regular sleep can be difficult to achieve. On those occasions, sleep practices are 
more effective and attainable when combined with mindfulness, which is another mental 
resilience practice.

Mindfulness 
In Unit 3, you were introduced to mindfulness. This is a growing practice that is not to be 
confused with meditation. Mindfulness is particularly effective in assisting your ability to 
focus. The CORE creators consider mindfulness to be (Fernandez et al., 2020: 8): 
• intentional; 
• present-focused; and 
• non-judgemental.  
Bearing these three key components in mind, mindfulness has been proven to impact the 
four resilience areas (Fernandez et al., 2020: 8). While there is still much to be explored in 
terms of research around mindfulness, studies have shown that practising mindfulness 
goes hand in hand with cognitive processes, and it helps with regard to learning, memory, 
self-awareness and focus (Fernandez et al., 2020: 8). The benefits of mindfulness in the 
workplace include an increase in job performance and social support, and a decrease in 
burnout and work pressure.  
 
It is reported that mindfulness also reduces stress, depression and anxiety, while 
contributing to the development of a leader’s abilities in the workplace, such as their 
creativeness, strength and self-improvement (Fernandez et al., 2020: 8). Daniel Goleman 
(2017: 37), one of the front runners in emotional intelligence research, suggests that 20 to 
30 minutes of mindfulness over the course of the day can result in optimal effectiveness. 
However, as with all of the practices suggested in this unit, the duration of practice is not as 
important as actually integrating the practice into your life. You can increase the duration of 
the various practices mentioned slowly over time. However, to begin, you should focus on 
incorporating them into your daily routine, making a habit of them and ensuring that you 
perform them in the correct way, with full attention and focus.  
 
The following examples demonstrate how you can practise mindfulness with minimal effort 
(Fernandez et al., 2020: 8): 
 
Start small: You can begin by integrating mindfulness into your life in small increments; for 
example, 30 or 60 seconds at a time in between your daily activities, after waking up or 
before going to bed.

Choose a sense: You can choose a sense and focus on it. Try picking the most active sense 
in that moment; for example, the smell of a candle, the sound of the wind or the warmth of 
the sun on your face.  
Incorporate mindfulness into your daily activities: Mindfulness requires you to simply 
dedicate a moment of your time to focus on the present. For example, while eating a meal, 
you can try to focus on the taste of your food, thereby immersing yourself in the moment. 
 
Reappraisal 
Of all the resilience practices suggested in the CORE framework, cognitive reappraisal is 
perhaps the most important, as well as the most effective. In a discussion about the nature 
of resilience, Neenan (2018: 2) focuses on the mental approach, discussing how resilience 
is about thinking in a flexible way, so that you can adapt when circumstances change. Most 
of us are familiar with the saying ‘mind over matter’ . This belief suggests that how we think 
can affect both our physiology and our behaviour greatly. Furthermore, our cognitive biases 
can sometimes cloud our judgement, and they can affect our ability to see things clearly. 
As an effective leader, it is essential to be able to recognise and monitor your cognitive 
behaviour and be aware of when you are being controlled by your automatic response 
systems and cognitive biases. 
To gain a clearer understanding of how we can improve our thinking about negative 
circumstances, Neenan (2018: 13) discusses how to distinguish 
between changeable and unchangeable situations. The following table summarises

The following suggestions provide alternative ways of incorporating and practising cognitive 
reappraisal more regularly (Fernandez et al., 2020: 9): 
• Pay attention to your self-talk: You should try to be mindful of the way you speak to 
yourself. Notice the thoughts that you have about yourself, as well as about 
situations and people.  
• Practise answering challenging questions: You can plan your day to include a period 
of self-reflection, where you practise answering challenging questions. During this 
period, which can be as short as five minutes, you can reflect on what happened, 
how you reacted in a certain situation and what you thought about the situation.

Unchangeable 
situation 
In this case, the situation is 
definite, and because you cannot 
take any action to alter the 
outcome, you must focus on your 
emotional reaction to the situation. 
Your supervisor hands you a letter of 
termination and a severance package. 
Here, action has already been taken (by 
the supervisor), and the situation (your

response should be to anticipate and

ensuring that your behaviour is not

Potentially 
changeable 
situation 
In this case, the situation may not 
be black-and-white. You may know 
that it is possible to change the 
situation or aspects of it; however, 
you are uncertain. Alternatively, 
you may be sure that the situation

what steps to take. 
Your supervisor calls you into their office

you are unsure of whether your

The uncertain nature of the situation

The following suggestions provide alternative ways of incorporating and practising cognitive 
reappraisal more regularly (Fernandez et al., 2020: 9): 
• Pay attention to your self-talk: You should try to be mindful of the way you speak to 
yourself. Notice the thoughts that you have about yourself, as well as about 
situations and people.  
• Practise answering challenging questions: You can plan your day to include a period 
of self-reflection, where you practise answering challenging questions. During this 
period, which can be as short as five minutes, you can reflect on what happened, 
how you reacted in a certain situation and what you thought about the situation.

• Help groups to examine assumptions: When in a group setting, such as a meeting, 
work team, or family or social gathering, you should be on the lookout for evidence 
of cognitive biases or distortions. As a leader, you can help your group to question 
their perspective; for example, by asking whether, as a group, you are missing key 
information.  
 
Savouring 
Savouring is the psychological practice of pursuing and focusing on positive things in your 
life as a way of promoting your psychological and physical health. However, it is important 
to note that this is not about trying to suppress or eradicate negative thoughts. Being aware 
of this distinction is important for a healthy mind, as studies have shown that trying to 
ignore or dismiss thoughts and emotions – both positive and negative – amplifies them 
instead (David and Congleton, 2013). For example, a negative emotion can be a warning 
against something that is harmful to you. For this reason, people tend to dwell on negative 
emotions more than on positive ones. This is referred to as negativity bias (Ruderman et al., 
2022). This can affect leadership negatively, as negativity bias increases insecurities and 
feelings of stress. However, savouring counteracts this. This is done by fostering a habit of 
focusing on the positive and diminishing the presence of negative bias, so that your 
decisions can be informed by rational observation. Furthermore, numerous studies have 
shown a correlation between positivity and life success in terms of finances, health and 
relationships (Ruderman et al., 2022). 
 
The following are three ways, among many others, in which to practise savouring 
(Ruderman et al., 2022):  
1. Share your good feelings: When sharing positive emotions with someone, do not 
stick to only the facts. Rather, you should elaborate on what happened and how it 
made you feel. This enables you to take the time to remember the positive 
experience.  
2. Congratulate yourself: You should take pride in your accomplishments, whether big 
or small, and congratulate yourself on that which you have done well.  
3. Take a mental picture: If you are undergoing a positive experience, you should try to 
capture the moment by taking a mental snapshot. This is a useful memory trick, but 
it also reinforces your acknowledgement of the special nature of that moment.

The effects of savouring can be increased by practising gratitude, which is another key 
component of positive psychology. 
 
Gratitude 
Practising gratitude is about identifying a positive thing, and then acknowledging the origin 
of that positive thing. In this way, like savouring, gratitude is about focusing on positive 
experiences. It also has many of the same benefits as savouring, such as an improvement 
in sleep quality, lower levels of anxiety and a lower susceptibility to illness (Kopans, 2017: 
43). In terms of leadership, practising gratitude is an effective way of improving your work 
relationships, as well as the general work performance and job satisfaction in your 
workplace (Ruderman et al., 2022). Making a habit of expressing gratitude can also help 
you to find meaning in various aspects of your life. Discovering purpose is an effective 
resilience resource, as it contributes to feelings of hope and determination, and it 
encourages a brighter outlook on the future (i.e. there is something to live for). In other 
words, it makes the present less overwhelming by shifting some of the focus to the future.  
 
The following can be done to help you practise gratitude (Kopans, 2017: 43; and Young, 
2022: 46): 
• Write gratitude notes: The next time someone does something nice for you, consider 
writing them a thank-you note. In the process, not only will you reinforce your own 
positive reaction, but you will also provide the other person with a positive 
experience of their own. 
• Keep journals and lists: Keeping written records of the things for which you are 
grateful is a great way of acknowledging a positive aspect or event in your life. It also 
provides you with a physical expression of positivity, which can be returned to 
whenever you are feeling burned out, depressed or lonely.  
• Perform gratitude rituals: This can involve making a habit of counting your blessings. 
As explained previously, people tend to focus on the negative things in life, and 
positive emotions are not always felt automatically. However, through practice, you 
can increase the frequency of positive emotions.  
As a resilience practice, expressing gratitude depends on you sharing your experiences 
with other people. This is where social connection becomes invaluable to a leader.

Social connection 
Social connection refers to the ability ‘to connect and relate to other human beings’ 
(Fernandez et al., 2020: 12). Resilience practices in terms of social connection involve 
focusing on and improving your interactions with other people, including friends, family 
members, co-workers and strangers. The benefits that you can receive from social 
connection are not dependent on meaningful, intimate or long-term connections – even a 
brief interaction with a stranger can have a positive effect on you (Fernandez et al., 2020: 
12). Unfortunately, reports of loneliness have doubled over the last few decades, and they 
continue to escalate, despite the instant communication provided by the current age of 
technology (Murthy, 2017). This can impact leaders, in particular, who often feel that they 
must be self-sufficient. However, it is important that, as a leader, you utilise and nurture 
the resources that are available to you, as well as the resources that are gained from social 
connections. 
The following are suggested ways to form meaningful connections (Murthy, 2017; and 
Fernandez et al., 2020: 12): 
• Reach out: When you are going through a difficult time, you can reach out to loved 
ones, friends, a co-worker or an acquaintance who may be sympathetic. 
Alternatively, you can be intentional about creating a strong support system, which 
can include valued mentors, co-workers and friends who can provide you with 
assistance or advice. 
• Understand others’ perspectives: Understanding those around you can improve 
your leadership abilities by helping you to re-evaluate your cognitive biases or 
behaviour. You should therefore try to get to know how your co-workers think or feel 
by asking them questions about themselves, so as to draw them into conversation. 
• Exercise your social muscle: Like most things in life, connecting with people is 
something that can be improved through practise. To begin, you can start out small 
by making a habit of greeting the people around you and asking how they are doing.

text_resource.text:
contact with those you care about is more beneficial than physical contact with strangers 
or co-workers. However, even a simple handshake with a stranger or high-five with a co-
worker can have a positive effect on your physiology. Studies have shown that social 
contact activates the vagus nerve – the part of your nervous system that slows down your 
heart rate and breathing (Field, 2010). In this way, social contact can help to counteract the 
harmful physiological effects that stress can have on the body (Field, 2010). 
The following can be done to increase contact, so as to strengthen your resilience 
(Ratschen et al., 2020; and Fernandez et al., 2020: 13): 
• Create a touch-support routine: You should aim to find ways to increase the 
frequency of physical contact in your life. For example, you can make a habit of 
hugging your family every time you greet them. 
• Cuddle your pets: If you live alone and have a pet, you can make sure to interact 
with them frequently; for example, by brushing them or giving them hugs.  
• Get a massage: The decreased pain and discomfort, and the increased relaxation, 
caused by a massage not only helps your stress levels, but it can also improve your 
attentiveness and boost your immune system. 
 
You have now been exposed to a diverse range of resilience practices and strategies that 
have been designed to be integrated easily into your daily life. Furthermore, the diversity of 
the strategies discussed shows how important it is for you to consider all four key resilience 
areas. By following the CORE framework and using these practices as a starting point, you 
can begin to cultivate your own resilience portfolio, so as to ensure that you have the 
resources, strength and wisdom to adapt effectively to any challenge that you may face in 
future leadership roles.

following activity does not have set answers, but we encourage you to work through it 
thoroughly to help you cultivate a comprehensive understanding of adaptive leadership in 
different contexts.

text_resource.text:
a. Cognitive reappraisal is a practice for both the mental and emotional 
resilience areas. 
b. Savouring belongs to the emotional resilience area. 
c. Sleep falls under both the physical and mental areas of resilience. 
d. Gratitude is a practice for both the emotional and social areas of resilience. 
e. Touch is a practice for both the social and physical resilience areas. 
ii. According to the CORE framework, savouring is a resilience practice that cultivates 
predominantly emotional resilience, while mindfulness is a resilience practice that 
cultivates predominantly mental resilience. Therefore, they are both resilience 
practices that are designed to support your psychological health. Furthermore, both 
practices involve focusing your thoughts and attention deliberately. However, with 
mindfulness, you are focusing your attention on the present moment in a non-
judgemental manner, whereas with savouring practices, you are focusing 
specifically on positive experiences either in the past or in the future. Examples of 
savouring techniques may include sharing your positive feelings, congratulating 
yourself and taking a mental picture of positive moments. Examples of mindfulness 
techniques may include starting and ending your day with mindfulness, 
incorporating mindfulness into your daily activities, and meditating through the use 
of an anchor, such as your breath or a sense. 
  
iii. False. While physical activity is an excellent way of combating stress effects by 
burning off excess energy and hormones, there are many other ways of either 
preventing or counteracting the negative effects of stress. For example, mindfulness 
and cognitive reappraisal techniques can help to prevent your stress levels from 
increasing in the moment, either by calming your body physically through 
meditation or by reappraising the threat level of the situation. Alternatively, after the 
intense periods of stress, simple things like getting a massage or sleeping soundly 
can help to calm the body and rebalance your hormone levels.

4.4 Theory in practice 
 
Now that you have developed your understanding of how to cultivate resilience in the 
context of adaptive leadership, it is time for you to see the theories put into practice. In the 
two real-life scenarios that follow, you will be presented with detailed examples of how this 
unit’s concepts and techniques have been applied to different adaptive leadership 
challenges.  
 
 
 
4.4.1 Example 4 A 
 
Andrew Collis is the chief financial officer (CFO) at Moneypenny, a global communications 
provider based in the United States (US) and United Kingdom (UK). Over the course of his 
career, Collis has faced many challenges. However, his ability to overcome these 
challenges is attributed to his optimistic outlook and his belief that adversity offers 
valuable opportunities for self-discovery and learning more about those around him. Collis 
defines resilience as the capacity to maintain composure in the face of life’s trials, and to 
employ healthy coping mechanisms to emerge even stronger. In other words, cognitive 
reappraisal is important to his success as a leader. Collis’s accomplishments as an 
adaptable and resilient leader can be attributed to a series of five key steps: 
1. Self-care: Collis prioritises his personal well-being through the implementation of 
CORE practices, including adequate sleep and regular physical activity.  
2. Forward focus: He embraces cognitive reappraisal practices by shifting the focus 
from dwelling on negative aspects to regarding change as a positive force.  
3. Continuous learning: He views life experiences as valuable lessons for personal 
growth, complemented by mindful reflection.  
4. Social engagement: He has cultivated social connections by actively engaging with 
others. 
5. Proactive leadership: Collis takes initiative in pursuing activities that contribute to 
him becoming a more effective leader; for example, evaluating a tricky situation, 
and then creating a plan of action to improve it.

Nelson Mandela’s life story serves as a powerful illustration of resilience and adaptive 
leadership, offering valuable lessons that are applicable to the corporate world. Also 
known as ‘Madiba’ , the former late South African president faced hardships in his lifetime. 
However, in more ways than one, he is still viewed as a resilient figure. As an anti-apartheid 
activist, the first black president and a key role player in the abolishment of racism and 
segregation in South Africa, Mandela exemplified the importance of resilience and 
adaptability. 
He possessed a unique ability to inspire people, foster reconciliation and meet the needs 
of his nation of followers. This required a profound understanding of his own motives, 
values, emotions and life purpose. In order to guide South Africa through turbulent times 
toward reconciliation, Mandela established strong social bonds with individuals who held 
diverse opinions, beliefs and backgrounds.  
Mandela’s strength and eagerness for change are evident in terms of the CORE resilience 
practices. He showed great perseverance through fighting against the injustices in our 
country, which resulted in his imprisonment. Mandela’s focus on social/political change 
pertains to cognitive reappraisal, as he noticed the positive rather than the negative. In 
other words, he fought for what was right, regardless of all the odds fighting against him.  
He also wrote his thoughts and experiences in a book, which can be considered self-talk 
and practising gratitude, and reflecting on one’s experiences. Mandela also practised 
social connection, as he encouraged his fellow captors in prison to fight alongside him in 
bringing about positive reformation. Moreover, Mandela’s leadership emphasises the 
importance of self-awareness as a key element of emotional intelligence. He recognised 
that true leadership begins with self-transformation, reflecting on the idea that leaders 
should be the change they wish to see. By embodying his ideals, Mandela inspired millions 
to dream big and to fight for a world that is characterised by hope.

Nelson Mandela’s life story serves as a powerful illustration of resilience and adaptive 
leadership, offering valuable lessons that are applicable to the corporate world. Also 
known as ‘Madiba’ , the former late South African president faced hardships in his lifetime. 
However, in more ways than one, he is still viewed as a resilient figure. As an anti-apartheid 
activist, the first black president and a key role player in the abolishment of racism and 
segregation in South Africa, Mandela exemplified the importance of resilience and 
adaptability. 
He possessed a unique ability to inspire people, foster reconciliation and meet the needs 
of his nation of followers. This required a profound understanding of his own motives, 
values, emotions and life purpose. In order to guide South Africa through turbulent times 
toward reconciliation, Mandela established strong social bonds with individuals who held 
diverse opinions, beliefs and backgrounds.  
Mandela’s strength and eagerness for change are evident in terms of the CORE resilience 
practices. He showed great perseverance through fighting against the injustices in our 
country, which resulted in his imprisonment. Mandela’s focus on social/political change 
pertains to cognitive reappraisal, as he noticed the positive rather than the negative. In 
other words, he fought for what was right, regardless of all the odds fighting against him.  
He also wrote his thoughts and experiences in a book, which can be considered self-talk 
and practising gratitude, and reflecting on one’s experiences. Mandela also practised 
social connection, as he encouraged his fellow captors in prison to fight alongside him in 
bringing about positive reformation. Moreover, Mandela’s leadership emphasises the 
importance of self-awareness as a key element of emotional intelligence. He recognised 
that true leadership begins with self-transformation, reflecting on the idea that leaders 
should be the change they wish to see. By embodying his ideals, Mandela inspired millions 
to dream big and to fight for a world that is characterised by hope.  
Mandela’s story demonstrates that individuals can develop emotional intelligence skills 
and embrace a framework that fosters resilience and adaptability. Despite facing many

Ethical Leadership as Process: A Conceptual Proposition
Fahad Shakeel, Peter Mathieu Kruyen and Sandra Van Thiel
Radboud University
This conceptual study proposes that ethical leadership is studied through a processual lens. The
study develops different models of ethical leadership as a process. Multiple constructs of ethical
leadership from the literature are compared and used to develop these models, including a time-
line of ethical leadership, a two-dimensional quadrant, and concentric circles of ethical leader-
ship. The models provide a new perspective into the function and interdependency of the
constituent parts to study ethical leadership as a process. The research agenda provides a road-
map for how these assumptions can be tested empirically, by looking into the external orientation
of leaders — for example, through administering a broader ethical leadership measurement tool.
This study calls for future research to test this assumption empirically, explore antecedent factors,
and study various historically important leaders through their actions and decisions to test if they
followed a leadership development path in accordance with the proposed model.
Keywords: concentric circles of ethical leadership, ethical leadership, ethical leadership process,
ethical leadership quadrant, ethical leadership timeline
Studies focusing on ethical leadership attribute its growing importance to the immoral and
unprofessional conduct of leaders that looms large nowadays, affecting both public and pri-
vate sector organizations. According to one report, forced turnover in the world top 2,500
largest public companies due to ethical lapses increased from 3.9% in 2007 –2011 to 5.3% in
2012–2016 (Rivera & Karlsson, 2017). However, ethical leadership crises are not new, and
the literature on ethical leadership has its roots in ancient as well as recent history and des-
pite decades of research, most papers are normative (Brown & Trevino, 2006; Shakeel,
Kruyen, & Van Thiel. 2018).
Ethics scholarship in general and ethical leadership literature in particular have sought to
highlight the significant role of ethics for leaders across sectors by conceptualizing ethical
leadership in different ways. For instance, the most basic model includes the prime dimen-
sions of the ethical virtues of the leaders themselves and activities that they undertake to
inculcate these into followers (Brown, Trevi ~no, & Harrison, 2005). Other models include

In the presence of such multiple constructs, the narrative of what constitutes ethical lead-
ership can be found through establishing common grounds; however, a broader perspective is
required to achieve it. A broader perspective on the interlinkages between constructs of eth-
ical leadership and related leadership styles suggests the possibility of their coexistence as a
process to achieve a common goal, higher ethical values in all styles of leadership. This art-
icle is intended as a conceptual study that attempts to answer the question of whether the
existing literature provides sufficient evidence for ethical leadership to be studied as a pro-
cess. If proven, such a processual perspective can help to explain whether ethical leadership
is constant or can develop over time —and if so how —and how it relates to other leadership
styles. This article is intended as purely argumentative; empirical validation is beyond the
scope of this article.
This study assumes that it is important to consider ethical leadership as a process and link
it to other leadership styles instead of regarding it as a leadership style of its own.
Comprehension as one distinguishable leadership style greatly undermines the role that ethics
play in all leadership theories and styles. Seeing ethical leadership as a process helps to con-
nect the ethical aspects of multiple leadership theories and thus broadens our scope of the
role that ethics plays within leadership at large. This article will present and illustrate a pat-
tern for the development of distinct ethical modes of leadership, which will provide import-
ant new opportunities for research into ethical leadership.
This study develops the debate of studying ethical leadership as a process by outlining
three building blocks as separate sections leading toward processual illustrative models. The
first building block contrasts definitions of ethical leadership by Brown et al. ( 2005) and a
broader classification by Van Wart ( 2014). This leads toward the second building block
which includes a new broader definition and timeline of ethical leadership. Third, a timeline
is presented in which ethical leadership develops through different steps. Lastly, this article
presents its conclusion and recommendations for the future.
THE FIRST BUILDING BLOCK: CONCEPTUALIZATIONS OF
ETHICAL LEADERSHIP
Ethical leadership has been conceptualized in different ways, but the definition put forward
by Brown et al. ( 2005) remains popular (see review by Shakeel et al., 2018). Brown et al.
(2005, p. 120) define ethical leadership as “the demonstration of normatively appropriate
conduct through personal action and interpersonal relationships, and the promotion of such
conduct to followers through two-way communication, reinforcement, and decision-making. ”
This definition implies two main roles of an ethical leader: the moral person and the moral
manager. The role of moral person refers to the ethical values of the leader him/herself,
whereas the moral manager refers to the activities that the leader undertakes to inculcate
such ethical values in followers. The definition stated above mentions three such activities:
communication, reinforcement, and decision making. In other studies (e.g., Heres &
Lasthuizen, 2012) empowerment is also considered as an integral part of the activities of

text_resource.text:
the moral manager (Den Hartog & De Hoogh 2009; Resick, Hanges, Dickson, &
Mitchelson, 2006).
However, the absence of empowerment from this definition is not the only shortcoming of
the ethical leadership conceptualization by Brown et al. ( 2005). Shakeel et al. ( 2018) identify
at least eight other shortcomings including negative reinforcement; vagueness in defining
stakeholders; vagueness in normative appropriateness; no attention for role clarification; no
reference to environmental sustainability; capacity for self-improvement; capacity for ethical
competence; and withholding necessary transformation (see also Den Hartog, 2015;
Eisenbeiss, 2012; Kalshoven et al., 2011a; Voegtlin, 2016). These limitations highlight the
shortcomings of ethical leadership as conceptualized by Brown et al. ( 2005) in definition,
construct, and lack of sufficient grounds to identify it as a separate style.
An alternative conceptualization of ethical leadership, which overcomes these shortcom-
ings, is the categorization of ethical leadership into constituent leadership styles by Van Wart
(2014). Van Wart lists six leadership styles as contemporary ethical leadership theories.
These styles are virtuous leadership; authentic and positive leadership; moral management;
professionally grounded leadership; social responsibility leadership; and transformational
leadership. These three classifications are also referred to as character; duty; and greatest
good, which are termed to be important for good leadership (as a process) to be robust. In
essence, this study argues that the constituent leadership styles of Van Wart can be placed on
a timeline reflecting a process in which every succeeding style is dependent on the comple-
tion ( “existence” in this case) of the preceding style. This is discussed in more detail in the
upcoming section.
THE SECOND BUILDING BLOCK: NEW DEFINITION AND TIMELINE
Based on the ideas of Van Wart ( 2014), Shakeel and colleagues presented a broader defin-
ition of ethical leadership incorporating the raised critical points:
Ethical leadership is the implicit and explicit pursuit of desired ethical behavior for self and
followers through efforts governed by rules and principles that advocate learning motivation,
healthy optimism and clarity of purpose to uphold the values of empowerment, service to
others, concern for human rights, change for betterment and fulfilling duties towards society,
future generations, environment and its sustainability. (Shakeel et al., 2018,p .9 )
This article will use this broader definition and the categorization of ethical leadership by
Van Wart ( 2014) to create a timeline of the ethical leadership process. This timeline shows
the primary difference in the scope of leadership in these related styles through varying focus
on external orientation. This external orientation of the leader moves from low to high exter-
nal orientation. (See Figure 1)
As explained earlier, ethical leadership styles differ from each other in the degree of exter-
nal orientation of the leader, as shown in Figure 1 . This points toward the possibility that
leaders can move from one style to the next by taking certain steps, which will be explained
in the next section. This section will first discuss the differences in external orientation
between the different styles, as illustrated in Table 1 .

Van Wart ( 2014) portrays virtuous leaders as ethical leaders who focus on their own
personal integrity. This conceptualization is similar to the moral person notion of Brown ’s
construct of ethical leadership. Brown et al. ( 2005) view a moral person as a leader who
has ethical qualities but makes no effort to inculcate these qualities in followers (which
according to their construct is the role of the moral manager) and instead focuses solely on
self-ethics.
Being a virtuous leader is the baseline model for ethical leadership. All succeeding roles
and styles have additional qualities. The attributes linked to the minimal virtue are honesty;
fairness; wisdom; acknowledgment of mistakes by the leader; opposition of unethical practi-
ces; conscientiousness and holding followers accountable (Brown et al., 2005; MacIntyre,
1981; Shakeel et al., 2018). In view of the self-focus of the virtuous leader, this type of lead-
ership is placed on the left side of the timeline of the ethical leadership process with low
external focus.
Authentic and positive leaders succeed virtuous leaders in the timeline as they are
assumed to be more externally oriented. The evidence of this external orientation lies in the
virtues associated with such leadership by scholars. It is also similar to the moral person
notion of Brown and colleagues ’ conceptualization of ethical leadership (Brown et al., 2005;
Van Wart, 2014). The attributes associated with these types of leadership are self-awareness;
self-improvement; open to feedback; positive influence on self and followers; and being non-
defensive. The attribute of openness to feedback and an attempt to influence followers

implies engagement with other actors, probably within the organization. This shows a higher
degree of external orientation than virtuous leadership.
Succeeding authentic and positive leadership in the time line of ethical leadership process
is the moral manager. It entails activities undertaken by managers to achieve desired ethical
outcomes. The attributes associated with moral manager are strict ethical compliance with
ethical mandates or organizational rules. The emphasis here is on compliance and reliance on
rules. The position of the moral manager on the time line stems from its role of guiding fol-
lowers toward ethical outcomes based on rules. It is more externally focused than the positive
leader who assesses himself based on an external benchmark (which implies self-correction)
and who attempts to influence followers, whereas the moral manager actively guides other
followers and hence interacts more with external actors in their goal toward achieving eth-
ical outcome.
Professionally grounded leadership is similar in nature as the moral manager. However, in
contrast to moral management, this leadership does not rely on rules and regulations to instill
ethics in followers, but instead focuses on legal and organizational principles. It is also asso-
ciated with the ability to interpret competing sources of authority and focus on aspiration
rather than rules (Van Wart, 2014). To clarify the distinction between the moral manager and
the professionally grounded leader, Shakeel et al. ( 2018) explain that if a leader makes a
decision based on rules, he/she would be following the Brown et al. ( 2005) notion of moral
management, but if he makes decisions which have no precedence or associating rule for
guidance, theoretically, she will be acting as a professionally grounded leader. Since princi-
ples are prospectively broader and more generalized than rules, this article assumes profes-
sionally grounded leaders to be more externally oriented than moral managers.
The next position in the timeline of ethical leadership is that of the socially responsible
leader which includes servant leadership, spiritual leadership, and corporate social responsibil-
ity (CSR). Servant leadership aims to serve the actors related to the organization and has care
and compassion as key attributes. Spiritual leaders see their work as a “higher calling” and dis-
play sacrificing behavior, whereas CSR focuses on the broader society and environment and
values sustainability (Turker, 2009; Van Wart, 2014). Since aspects of socially responsible
leaders show a greater focus (through acts like sacrifice) on follower development and aspects
beyond organization including society and environment, they are considered to have more
external orientation compared to the leadership styles discussed earlier. A more precise distinc-
tion between servant and spiritual leadership is beyond the scope of this study, but it empha-
sizes the distinction between these two and CSR, which, as indicated by the title, focuses on
actors beyond the organization including the broader society and environment.
Van Wart ( 2014) considers transformational leadership the “proper ends” of ethical leader-
ship. Other ethical leadership studies, such as that of Brown et al. ( 2005), characterized the
overlap between the conceptualization of ethical leadership and transformational leadership
partial at best. However, this article stresses the central role in ethical propagation of trans-
formational leadership attributes, such as undertaking actual changes within organizations to
adapt to growing needs of the organization as well as society —for example, the transition to
environmentally friendly methods of doing business (sustainability). On this basis, it can be
seen as an important outcome of the process and assume it as the highest externally orien-
tated form of ethical leadership.

THE THIRD BUILDING BLOCK: STEPS OF THE ETHICAL
LEADERSHIP PROCESS
The process in which leaders ’ external orientation increases and leaders can move from one
form of ethical leadership to the next on the time line depends on their taking specific steps.
This is illustrated in Figure 2 .
Figure 2 shows a process consisting of six broad steps, which are associated with the
corresponding leadership styles from Figure 1 . Again, the order of the steps depicts an
increasing external orientation. This implies that ethical leadership development starts with
self-focus, grows into utmost dedication toward followers and other external factors, and con-
cludes into commitment to initiating change of the status quo.
The first step of the process starts with individual ethics, and the role of the leader is to
focus on developing ethical skills. The source of adopting an ethical lifestyle could be exter-

THE THIRD BUILDING BLOCK: STEPS OF THE ETHICAL

The process in which leaders ’ external orientation increases and leaders can move from one

corresponding leadership styles from Figure 1 . Again, the order of the steps depicts an
increasing external orientation. This implies that ethical leadership development starts with
self-focus, grows into utmost dedication toward followers and other external factors, and con-
cludes into commitment to initiating change of the status quo.

text_resource.text:
managers are both assumed to govern employees toward ethical behavior through their func-
tional roles. It is also probable that they cater to the same extent of external actors. However,
in this step principles guide a leader ’s behavior more than rules. This competency can indi-
cate being governed by such guidelines that include both aspirational codes and operational
assistance (Meine & Dunn, 2013). In a study that attempts to distinguish between rules and
principles, Braithwaite ( 2002) asserts that when the type of action that needs to be regulated
is simple, stable, and does not involve huge economic interests, rules tend to regulate with
greater certainty than principles (Braithwaite, 2002, p. 75), whereas when the type of action
to be regulated is complex, changing, and involves large economic interests, principles tend
to regulate with greater certainty than rules (Braithwaite, 2002, p. 75).
This step does not imply that following principles depicts a higher moral position com-
pared to following rules alone; instead it reflects the increased focus on external orientation.
There are no studies that have empirically proven higher moral grounds for individuals pos-
sessing or following certain ethical principles. The intent to separate the two steps is focused
solely on the specificity and generic nature of the two in terms of external orientation as
stated in Braithwaite ( 2002).
As problems best solved through principles are more complex than those best solved by
rules, it is safe to assume that grounded leaders are trained and developed more in terms of
new skills learned to handle complex problems. For a moral manager to handle complex
problems, she will need these added skills and experience. Such skills relate to ethical com-
petence (Shakeel et al., 2018)—an aspect that can be addressed through leaders ’ learning.
The fifth step in the ethical leadership process is related to leadership behavior that is pre-
dominantly focused on the self-actualization of followers, and how the leader can help them
to achieve their goals. This implies a certain servitude or even sacrifice on the part of the
leader and his utmost dedication toward his followers and the broader social environment.
Finally, the last step of the ethical leadership process is concerned with achieving change,
which can be both inside and outside the organization, of the organizational culture, as well
as change aimed at achieving ethical needs outside of the organization. In this step, a leader
will develop and implement a plan of action to achieve changes that are considered necessary
from an ethics perspective.
This sequence is an incomplete mapping of numbered leadership styles and does not rep-
resent an exhaustive list of such. Moreover, the distinctions between the styles are merely
educated arguments to feed the processual discussion within this domain and remain to be
proved empirically.

international businesses use raw materials or import finished goods from developing coun-
tries, and the production of those materials or goods involves child labor, the leader can
decide to ignore this. He would then be following the laws of his own organization —and
thus be an ethical leader —but at the same time, his behavior could also be considered to be
not very ethical from a wider perspective.
Studies into ethical leadership are now exploring the dark sides of ethical leadership. In
their review, Shakeel, Kruyen and Van Thiel ( 2016) discuss studies that attribute the negative
effects of ethical leadership to an overemphasis on ethics. This can lead to, for example,
moral over-exhaustion (Zheng et al., 2015) or unethical pro-organizational behavior (UPB)
(Miao et al., 2013; Mo & Shi, 2017).
The existence of this dark side raises questions regarding the process of ethical leadership
presented so far. To discuss this, a two- dimensional quadrant ( Figure 4 ) is presented here.
The x- axis of this illustration comes from the timeline of ethical leadership, and indicates
the level of external orientation from low to high. The y-axis indicates the level of ethics por-
trayed through the leader behavior, also ranging from low (negative) to high (positive).
Together, this leads to four quadrants, each of which is supposed to represent a different
leadership role.
The low-left hand quadrant depicts a narcissistic unethical leader, who has low values on
ethics and serves only his self-interest. The high-left hand quadrant points to a virtuous
leader, who follows ethical discourse herself, but is not concerned with the external environ-
ment or her followers. The high-right hand quadrant depicts an ethical transformational
leader, who not only limits herself to follower guidance, but also undertakes implementation

of a wider discourse for ethical causes. The low-right hand quadrant points to an unethical
pseudotransformation leader, who uses external and internal actors within the organization,
and/or implements a wider agenda to fulfill selfish schemes. Pseudotransformational leaders
are described as those who “advance their own self-interested agendas by dominating and
controlling their followers. In focusing on self-interest, pseudo-transformational leaders are
more interested in becoming personal idols than in the collective ideals that might benefit
their followers” (Bass & Steidlmeier, 1999, cited in Barling et al., 2008, p. 852).
Figure 4 also shows the moral manager and professional grounded leadership in the
middle. This is because: (a) there are no studies that explore the dark side for these styles
(for either of them), and (b) ethical leadership conceptualization (with a focus on moral
management) is also predicted to use multiple styles based on their role and the nature of
the organization that they serve (Heres & Lasthuizen, 2012). Earlier, a difference was dis-
cussed between moral managers and grounded leaders (following Van Wart, 2014), which
showed that moral managers focus more on rules and grounded leaders more on princi-
ples. It could be argued that in the initial stages of follower guidance, leaders make more
use of ethical rules, and hence, the role of moral management is more dominant in the
start of the process. This is shown by placing the moral management toward the left side
in the figure. Toward the end of the process, when leaders are required to solve ethical
dilemmas and implement an ethical discourse, professionally grounded leadership is
assumed to play a more active role. This is shown by placing grounded leadership toward
the right side of the figure.
The quadrant does not include all ethical leadership styles. More elaboration is necessary
but beyond the scope of this contribution. More recommendations for future research are
offered in the final section of this article.
DISCUSSION AND RESEARCH AGENDA
Ethical leadership was seen as a distinct style by scholars like Brown et al. ( 2005), but the
categorization of ethical leadership into constituent styles by Van Wart ( 2014) has paved the
way for ethical leadership to be studied as a process with different steps of development.
Such a processual approach can also be helpful in explaining the relationship between the
different styles of ethical leadership. The interdependence of these constituent styles on each
other for their smooth functioning is also testimonial to the processual approach. Just as the
moral management cannot completely function to its desired capacity if the moral person
(similar to virtuous leadership) is not present (Brown et al., 2005); in a similar way, trans-
formational leadership cannot achieve its desired outcome unless virtuous leadership qualities
are also present. This study asserts that the presence of pseudotransformational leaders also
adds evidence to this assumption.
Moreover, the linkage of leadership theory to learning (Brown & Posner, 2001) further
validates that leadership can be a similar process of continued learning and adapting to the
new challenges. The quadrant and the concentric circles of ethical leadership shown in this
study help understand the process and indicate that ethical leadership can be seen as a pro-
cess instead of a distinct style of its own, but additional empirical studies are needed to

622 SHAKEEL ET AL.

text_resource.text:
validate this conclusion. This study is not without its limitations. The timeline of ethical lead-
ership lists only a few related ethical leadership styles and is not an exhaustive list.
Furthermore, it is certainly not asserted that transformational leadership is the end of this pro-
cess. As leadership is associated with learning (Brown & Posner, 2001), which is an ongoing
and continuous process, the implementation of required ethical transformational changes lead
to the resumption of the process from one of the stages again. This model fails to indicate
when the process restarts; more research is needed to verify this proposition.
In a similar pattern, the quadrants show only numbered styles, and offer a limited account
of corresponding negative attitudes. The corresponding negative side to grounded leadership
or moral management is not part of the model, due to lack of credible research evidence.
These aspects warrant further research to develop this model.
Future research can focus on various aspects of the process. The process of ethical leader-
ship with the proposed model can be empirically proven by validating the broader ethical
leadership scale developed by Shakeel et al. ( 2018). This can help verify the processual
nature of ethical leadership and will help establish the validity of ethical leadership as a pro-
cess. For the empirical results to prove the process true, individuals ’ external orientation
scores should depict a pattern similar to that of the sequence on the timeline. Future studies
could also explore whether rules indeed fit best for lower management levels and principles
for higher management levels because of more complexity of decisions at the top.
Alternatively, it could be studied whether the effect and use of ethical rules and principles
are different for different sectors (e.g., public versus private sector).
Another line of inquiry could be related to antecedent factors of ethical leadership.
Although previous research into ethical leadership has established linkages to personality
traits (Kalshoven, Den Hartog, & De Hoogh, 2011b; Walumbwa & Schaubroeck, 2009; Xu,
Yu, & Shi, 2011); in terms of our model, interesting avenues include discovering which per-
sonality traits are related, or necessary, to various steps along the timeline of ethical leader-
ship. This could also help in tailored leader-development training programs for leaders along
these steps. Studies can also explore where historically important political and apolitical per-
sonalities stood in their development stage as leaders by studying their decisions and impact
on followers. For example, it would be interesting to know if Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was
ethically transformational; Mahatma Gandhi a servant; and Mother Teresa a spiritual leader,
and if they followed a leader development path visible through their actions and decisions in
accordance with the model proposed through this paper.
